meta.title: Find your first research question
meta.scorePolicy: Source scores and ranks use different rubrics and are not comparable between collections. There is no combined ranking.
meta.readinessPolicy: Starting-scope suggestions based on the source proposals, not launch approval or evidence from student pilots. Start means a proposed beginner entry; mentor means preparation or setup; rework means the research framing needs revision.
meta.trackPolicy: Tracks suggest interests, not eligibility or restrictions on who can choose a project. Open means either background or a new direction.
meta.publicationPolicy: Publication paths are conditional proposals. No idea has a guaranteed paper or a completed novelty check.
meta.literaturePolicy: References and source review claims are inherited from the two campaigns. Fable reports generator metadata checks and no full-text reading; Astra records abstract-level checks. This integration did not independently recheck the literature.
meta.costPolicy: Resource and budget figures are original proposal estimates, not current quotes or approved spending.
meta.overlapPolicy: All 200 proposals are retained with distinct source IDs. Shared themes help browse related work; similar proposals are not silently merged.

fieldNotes.baseline: Fable supplies its ground-truth/checking plan in this field; Astra supplies an explicit baseline.
fieldNotes.pivot: Fable uses its audit sharpening recommendation when present, otherwise a clearly generic planning suggestion.
fieldNotes.hook: Fable uses the first sentence of its original pitch, shortened with an ellipsis if necessary.
fieldNotes.question: Fable questions are concise editorial restatements; the full original pitch is preserved in experiment and originalAssessment.

ideas.title: When does one page become the whole database?
ideas.question: Does displaying an explicit remaining-item count reduce premature stopping more than a continuation cursor alone?
ideas.hook: A shopping assistant can miss the cheapest item simply because it never opens page two.
ideas.firstMonth: Learn Python lists and JSON; implement a 100-item catalog with pagination and produce a completeness-versus-page-size plot on 30 generated tasks.
ideas.experiment: Hold catalog and requested optimum fixed; vary page size, answer location, cursor wording, and remaining-count visibility. Measure exhaustive-search completion, optimum regret, calls, and incorrect claims of completeness.
ideas.baseline: A deterministic cursor-following loop supplies exact answers; compare plain agent, count display, and mandatory pagination wrapper at equal call budgets.
ideas.publicationPath: If count visibility explains failures across two catalog domains, release a small interface experiment and cost-sensitive completion rule, then validate on a public tool benchmark.
ideas.risk: Pagination handling is standard engineering. Contribution must be the causal stopping behavior and overhead boundary, not invention of pagination or generic tool robustness.
ideas.pivot: If agents already exhaust pages, increase realistic result volume; if the wrapper always dominates, report the simpler engineering solution.
ideas.resources: Laptop, synthetic catalogs, at most 300 short inference runs; mentor supplies one API-call example, no custom agent framework.

ideas.title: An empty search is not a proof of absence
ideas.question: Can a coverage field help an agent distinguish no matching records from a search that examined only part of the records?
ideas.hook: A library assistant should not declare a book nonexistent after searching one shelf.
ideas.firstMonth: Create 40 tiny search tasks with exact answer keys and three legal tool responses: exhaustive empty, filtered empty, and incomplete empty.
ideas.experiment: Randomize matched response length and result contents while exposing or hiding coverage metadata. Measure correct absence claims, unnecessary extra searches, and false certainty at a fixed search budget.
ideas.baseline: An explicit three-state rule engine and exhaustive scan establish achievable behavior; compare natural-language coverage with a typed completeness flag.
ideas.publicationPath: A transferable calibration curve could justify a compact tool-response contract for trustworthy negative answers, conditional on replication across retrieval and inventory tasks.
ideas.risk: Abstention and incomplete retrieval are established problems. The narrow distinction is coverage semantics with identical empty payloads, not a new hallucination benchmark.
ideas.pivot: If a simple flag removes all errors, package the minimal contract; if errors depend only on missing knowledge, drop the proposed semantic mechanism.
ideas.resources: Laptop, generated records, 200–300 calls; beginner needs dictionaries and simple proportions, with a mentor reviewing labels.

ideas.title: How much error feedback actually teaches repair?
ideas.question: Does a constraint-specific counterexample improve argument repair beyond merely naming the failed argument?
ideas.hook: A useful error message tells you how to fix a form instead of saying something went wrong.
ideas.firstMonth: Implement five small validation tools and 50 invalid calls; create matched error templates without changing the underlying failures.
ideas.experiment: Randomize feedback among generic error, field name, violated predicate, and minimal counterexample. Keep token counts approximately matched; measure one-step repair, newly introduced errors, and transfer to unseen predicates.
ideas.baseline: A parser plus deterministic repair handles syntactic faults; oracle predicate checks grade semantic arguments, and copyable answer leakage is explicitly removed.
ideas.publicationPath: If predicate feedback generalizes, contribute an error-message design study distinguishing genuine repair from answer copying, with a small public invalid-call corpus.
ideas.risk: Failing Tools and existing recovery benchmarks already inject runtime errors. Novelty depends on causal information content and held-out constraint transfer, not recovery-rate reporting.
ideas.pivot: If gains vanish after answer leakage is removed, report the leakage result and avoid claiming improved reasoning.
ideas.resources: Laptop, JSON schemas, up to 300 calls; mentor provides a validator example; student learns exceptions and paired comparisons.

ideas.title: Units that fail only at the boundary
ideas.question: When an API mixes unit conversion with a strict threshold, does supplying a canonical-unit field prevent incorrect boundary decisions?
ideas.hook: Confusing grams and kilograms is easy to spot; rounding just across a limit is more deceptive.
ideas.firstMonth: Build a parcel-size checker with generated masses and lengths concentrated around admissibility boundaries; learn units, floating-point tolerances, and test cases.
ideas.experiment: Cross unit system, decimal precision, and distance from threshold while holding underlying physical values fixed. Measure accepted invalid parcels, rejected valid parcels, and conversion errors separately.
ideas.baseline: A decimal-arithmetic converter and exact inequality checker supply ground truth; compare raw fields, redundant canonical values, and executable validation.
ideas.publicationPath: If failures concentrate predictably near thresholds across two domains, publish a boundary-focused interface audit with an explicit error decomposition.
ideas.risk: Unit conversion and schema normalization are familiar. The contribution would be locating the interaction between representation precision and decision margins, not demonstrating that agents dislike units.
ideas.pivot: If all mistakes are plain arithmetic, pivot to a compact regression suite rather than a model-mechanism claim.
ideas.resources: Laptop and synthetic quantities; 250 calls; mentor checks dimensional consistency once; freshman learns arithmetic, loops, and plotting.

ideas.title: Can an agent explain a partly successful bulk action?
ideas.question: Does an itemized result table prevent an agent from describing a partially completed batch as entirely complete?
ideas.hook: An assistant that updates eight of ten tasks should tell you which two remain.
ideas.firstMonth: Implement a local ten-item checklist API with deterministic mixed outcomes; generate 40 requests and exact final-state summaries.
ideas.experiment: Vary failed-item position, batch size, and response format while keeping accepted items fixed. Score statement-level precision, unresolved-item recall, and unnecessary follow-up actions.
ideas.baseline: A template renderer over item statuses gives a perfect non-LLM report; compare free text, JSON statuses, and an enforced reconciliation table.
ideas.publicationPath: A useful result would separate state-tracking errors from report-generation errors and show when structured reporting earns its token cost.
ideas.risk: Partial failures and duplicate-side-effect recovery are well studied. This experiment freezes execution and examines truthful item-level communication, never claiming retry novelty.
ideas.pivot: If direct template rendering always suffices, the contribution is a clear boundary for removing the model from status reporting.
ideas.resources: Laptop, synthetic checklist state, 200 calls; mentor supplies a sample JSON trace; beginner learns set differences and exact scoring.

ideas.title: The cost of a guard that says no too often
ideas.question: At equal unsafe-action rates, does a minimal executable policy guard preserve more valid task completions than a blanket refusal prompt?
ideas.hook: A reliable assistant needs to finish ordinary jobs as well as avoid forbidden ones.
ideas.firstMonth: Write a toy reservation policy with three explicit predicates and enumerate valid/invalid requests; produce the first utility-versus-violation plot.
ideas.experiment: Vary policy exception frequency and linguistic ambiguity. Compare prompted caution with a guard that checks only formalized predicates; measure violations, unnecessary refusals, recovery calls, and valid completion.
ideas.baseline: A deterministic policy interpreter supplies labels; an always-refuse policy and unguarded agent bound the tradeoff, with identical tools and task budgets.
ideas.publicationPath: Conditional publication requires a reproducible refusal-cost analysis and evidence that gains persist when policy wording changes without changing its logic.
ideas.risk: Executable guards are established, and ToolEmu studies agent risk. The narrow question is overrestriction cost on matched policy exceptions, not a novel safety architecture.
ideas.pivot: If guards require a mentor to formalize every new task, constrain claims to the small policy class and release a teaching benchmark.
ideas.resources: Laptop, synthetic reservations, up to 300 calls; mentor checks the three predicates, student owns generation and evaluation.

ideas.title: Which read-back is worth paying for?
ideas.question: Can a field-difference rule allocate verification calls more efficiently than verifying every write in a small stateful workflow?
ideas.hook: Double-checking every action is safe but wastes time; checking nothing can hide mistakes.
ideas.firstMonth: Build a toy contact-book simulator with exact state and a two-call verification budget; enumerate 30 workflows and an oracle audit allocation.
ideas.experiment: Vary the number of modified fields, visibility of expected changes, and limited silent-update failures. Compare allocation rules using missed discrepancies and extra calls at equal successful-write counts.
ideas.baseline: Always-check, never-check, random checking, and a deterministic expected-diff rule are mandatory; simulator state supplies the full discrepancy set.
ideas.publicationPath: Only pursue a methods paper if a cheap observable predicts verification value on held-out workflow templates; otherwise release the allocation testbed and negative result.
ideas.risk: Verification after silent failures is already covered by Failing Tools. This asks which check to buy under a fixed audit budget, not whether checking helps.
ideas.pivot: If discrepancy risk is uniform and random checking matches all rules, reject the predictive allocation hypothesis.
ideas.resources: Laptop, generated workflows, 300 calls; mentor helps compute a tiny exhaustive oracle; prerequisites are sets and conditional probabilities.

ideas.title: Cancel requested versus cancel confirmed
ideas.question: Does an explicit operation-state diagram reduce premature cancellation claims when a tool acknowledges a request before completing it?
ideas.hook: Pressing cancel on a download does not always mean it has already stopped.

ideas.experiment: Vary acknowledgement wording, completion delay, and available status queries. Measure premature confirmed-cancellation claims, polling cost, and unnecessary repeated cancel requests.

ideas.publicationPath: If transition visibility improves both reporting and query efficiency across job and booking simulations, release a protocol comprehension benchmark and minimal interface guidance.

ideas.pivot: If errors disappear with a single unambiguous state name, keep the result as a focused design replication rather than a broad reliability claim.
ideas.resources: Laptop, synthetic queues, at most 250 calls; mentor provides a state-machine diagram, student implements and checks it.

ideas.title: The right name, the wrong record
ideas.question: Does requiring an exact identifier read-back prevent wrong-record edits when several search hits have nearly identical display names?
ideas.hook: Two people can share a name; an assistant should not update the first matching contact.
ideas.firstMonth: Generate a fake address book with controlled name collisions; implement search, inspect, and update tools and 40 reversible tasks.
ideas.experiment: Vary collision count, distinguishing-field position, and whether the tool returns an exact-ID confirmation step. Measure wrong-target edits, clarification frequency, and total calls.
ideas.baseline: An exact-key resolver with a required distinguishing attribute supplies the reference; ambiguous tasks are scored as clarification-required, not guessed.
ideas.publicationPath: A publishable extension would show a predictable collision-versus-cost curve and a confirmation strategy transferring from contacts to file selection.
ideas.risk: Entity disambiguation is mature. The proposed contribution is the action boundary between fuzzy retrieval and exact mutation, with an explicit ambiguity oracle.
ideas.pivot: If errors reflect missing user information only, report that limit and remove claims that an interface fix resolves irreducible ambiguity.
ideas.resources: Laptop, fabricated names only, 250 calls; mentor reviews the ambiguity labels; student learns keys, lookup tables, and confusion matrices.

ideas.title: Which logical words survive memory compression?

ideas.pivot: If errors occur equally without compression, reject a memory-writing explanation and inspect the decision reader instead.

ideas.title: The telephone game inside a memory summary
ideas.question: Does repeated summary-of-summary writing distort event order faster than regenerating an equal-length summary from original event records?
ideas.hook: Repeatedly retelling a story can change it even when nobody adds new facts.
ideas.firstMonth: Generate 30 event sequences with a known order; run one, three, and five compression cycles and visualize the first point where ordering changes.
ideas.experiment: Match final token budgets and number of model calls; vary event density and causal links. Measure pairwise order inversions, invented events, and downstream planning errors.
ideas.baseline: A timestamp-sorted event table and a fresh-from-source summary are required; controlled extraction provides an inexpensive non-LLM baseline.
ideas.publicationPath: If recursive summarization has a reproducible excess error, contribute a memory-maintenance study and a measured refresh schedule, then replicate on a public conversation subset.

ideas.title: How Many Runs Before You Trust a Benchmark Score?
ideas.question: How many repeated runs make an agent benchmark score trustworthy?
ideas.hook: Rerun a fixed cheap-LLM agent 20-50 times per condition on a small exact-match benchmark and fit the empirical score-variance vs run-count curve to get a minimum-n rule for a target confidence-interval width.
ideas.firstMonth: Week1: pick a 50-item exact-match benchmark, wire DeepSeek/Qwen API calls with logging. Week2: run 20 repeats at temp=0 and temp=0.7, log a per-item pass/fail matrix. Week3: bootstrap CI width vs n and compare to the binomial-noise prediction. Week4: write up a minimum-n table and the first CI-width-vs-n plot.
ideas.experiment: Rerun a fixed cheap-LLM agent 20-50 times per condition on a small exact-match benchmark and fit the empirical score-variance vs run-count curve to get a minimum-n rule for a target confidence-interval width. Surprising question: does the variance shrink like sqrt(n) i.i.d. noise, or plateau because failures are bimodal/structured rather than random?
ideas.baseline: Exact-match/regex grading against known-correct answers; variance estimated by bootstrap over logged repeats — fully machine-checkable.
ideas.publicationPath: Extend to 3 models x 3 benchmarks x controlled repeat budget; publish a practical 'minimum-n calculator' plus the empirical finding that variance floors are benchmark-specific, not model-specific. Target: NeurIPS Datasets & Benchmarks workshop or COLM.
ideas.risk: Cheap APIs may cache or be near-deterministic at temp=0, masking the true run-to-run variance we are trying to measure.
ideas.pivot: Use the first month to test whether the proposed comparison is feasible and distinct from earlier work; discuss scope changes with a mentor.
ideas.resources: ~¥300-500 API credits (DeepSeek/Qwen), laptop only.

ideas.title: Same Brain, Different Body: Harness Effects on Agent Accuracy
ideas.question: How much does an agent's surrounding software change its accuracy?
ideas.hook: Run one fixed model through 3-4 minimal agent harnesses (bare ReAct loop, JSON-schema-strict tool calling, no-scratchpad baseline) on the same tool-use tasks, holding prompt content and tools fixed.
ideas.firstMonth: Week1: pick a fixed toy tool-use task set (calculator + lookup-table tasks) and one model. Week2: hand-implement two harnesses (bare-loop vs strict-schema). Week3: run both on the task set, log accuracy, token cost, and failure modes. Week4: first bar chart of accuracy-by-harness with repeat-based error bars.
ideas.experiment: Run one fixed model through 3-4 minimal agent harnesses (bare ReAct loop, JSON-schema-strict tool calling, no-scratchpad baseline) on the same tool-use tasks, holding prompt content and tools fixed. Surprising question: how much of published 'agent capability' is actually harness engineering rather than model capability?
ideas.baseline: Fixed tool-use tasks with programmatic checkers (e.g., calculator/lookup result correctness).
ideas.publicationPath: Scale to 4 harnesses x 3 models x 2 task families and identify which harness design choices (retry policy, schema strictness, scratchpad) explain the most score variance. Target: EMNLP Findings or NeurIPS D&B workshop.
ideas.risk: Too many confounded design choices between harnesses at once; needs careful one-change-at-a-time ablation to isolate cause.
ideas.pivot: Use the first month to test whether the proposed comparison is feasible and distinct from earlier work; discuss scope changes with a mentor.

ideas.title: Shuffle Test: Row/Header Invariance for Data-Analysis Agents
ideas.question: Should rearranging a table change a data-analysis agent's answer?
ideas.hook: Give a data-analysis agent the same question about a CSV, permuting row order, column order, and header names (synonyms/random tokens) where the true answer cannot change, and measure how often its answer flips anyway.
ideas.firstMonth: Week1: build 10 synthetic CSVs (50-200 rows) with a fixed aggregation question (e.g., highest-mean category) with a programmatically known answer. Week2: write a permutation generator (row shuffle / column shuffle / header rename). Week3: run a cheap-LLM code-writing agent on all permutations x3 repeats. Week4: heatmap of accuracy drop by perturbation type.
ideas.experiment: Give a data-analysis agent the same question about a CSV, permuting row order, column order, and header names (synonyms/random tokens) where the true answer cannot change, and measure how often its answer flips anyway. Surprising question: which perturbation breaks accuracy most, and does the drop correlate with context length?
ideas.baseline: Synthetic CSVs with programmatically computed exact answers; permutations are answer-preserving by construction.
ideas.publicationPath: Extend to real messy datasets and full agent tool-use, defining a 'permutation robustness score' as a new evaluation axis. Target: ACL/EMNLP Findings or an evaluation-benchmark workshop.
ideas.risk: If the agent's code-execution tool re-sorts or re-derives the data internally, it can hide the very sensitivity being measured — tool access must be controlled.
ideas.pivot: Use the first month to test whether the proposed comparison is feasible and distinct from earlier work; discuss scope changes with a mentor.
ideas.resources: Free (local pandas + cheap API), laptop.

ideas.title: The Cost-Accuracy Frontier of Cheap LLM APIs on One Fixed Task
ideas.question: Which inexpensive model offers the best accuracy for a fixed budget?
ideas.hook: Sweep model choice (DeepSeek/Qwen/GLM/Kimi, mini vs full tiers), max-tokens, and reasoning-effort settings on one fixed benchmark, logging exact per-call cost, and plot the empirical accuracy-vs-cost Pareto frontier.
ideas.firstMonth: Week1: pick a fixed 50-item exact-match benchmark and record 4 providers' current pricing. Week2: build a runner that logs tokens and cost per call. Week3: run all model/setting combinations x3 repeats. Week4: first cost-vs-accuracy scatter plot with the Pareto frontier drawn.
ideas.experiment: Sweep model choice (DeepSeek/Qwen/GLM/Kimi, mini vs full tiers), max-tokens, and reasoning-effort settings on one fixed benchmark, logging exact per-call cost, and plot the empirical accuracy-vs-cost Pareto frontier. Surprising question: is the frontier smooth, or are there price 'cliffs' where a small cost increase buys a disproportionate accuracy jump?
ideas.baseline: Exact-match/programmatic grading; cost computed from published, dated, verifiable per-token pricing.
ideas.publicationPath: Extend across 3 task types (math, code, extraction) to test whether the frontier shape is task-dependent; publish a practical 'which cheap API for which job' benchmark. Target: NeurIPS D&B workshop or arXiv + lab report.
ideas.risk: Provider pricing and rate limits change frequently, threatening reproducibility; pricing snapshot dates must be recorded alongside every run.
ideas.pivot: Use the first month to test whether the proposed comparison is feasible and distinct from earlier work; discuss scope changes with a mentor.
ideas.resources: ~¥800 API credits across 4 providers, laptop.

ideas.title: Does Rewording the Question Change the Answer? A Paraphrase Audit
ideas.question: Does asking the same question differently change the answer?
ideas.hook: Generate 5 meaning-preserving paraphrases of each of 30 objectively-gradable questions and measure how often a target model's answer flips across paraphrases of the same underlying question.
ideas.firstMonth: Week1: pick 30 objectively-gradable questions. Week2: LLM-generate 5 paraphrases per question with a second-model meaning-preservation check. Week3: run the target model on all 180 (question, paraphrase) pairs x2 repeats. Week4: first flip-rate histogram per question.
ideas.experiment: Generate 5 meaning-preserving paraphrases of each of 30 objectively-gradable questions and measure how often a target model's answer flips across paraphrases of the same underlying question. Surprising question: is paraphrase-sensitivity concentrated in a few brittle questions, or spread evenly, and does it track question difficulty?
ideas.baseline: Exact-match grading against a fixed correct answer per original question; paraphrase meaning-preservation double-checked by a second model plus a spot human check.
ideas.publicationPath: Extend to multiple models and correlate a per-model 'paraphrase robustness score' with published leaderboard rankings, showing some ranking gaps are wording artifacts. Target: EMNLP Findings or an evaluation workshop.
ideas.risk: Automated paraphrase generation can silently shift question difficulty or meaning; needs an explicit meaning-preservation check step before scoring flips.

ideas.title: Fantastically Ordered Tool Calls: Does Exemplar Order Still Matter?
ideas.question: Does the order of examples change how an agent uses tools?
ideas.hook: Permute the order of a fixed set of worked tool-call exemplars in an agent's system prompt and measure accuracy variance across orderings on a tool-use benchmark.
ideas.firstMonth: Week1: build a 4-exemplar tool-use prompt template and a 30-item eval set. Week2: generate a sampled set of exemplar orderings. Week3: run each ordering x3 repeats on 2 cheap models. Week4: box plot of accuracy by ordering with the best-vs-worst gap reported.
ideas.experiment: Permute the order of a fixed set of worked tool-call exemplars in an agent's system prompt and measure accuracy variance across orderings on a tool-use benchmark. ideas.publicationPath: Extend across model families and exemplar-selection (not just order) to add an 'ordering sensitivity' axis to agent evaluation. Target: ACL/EMNLP Findings.
ideas.risk: Modern instruction-tuned models may show a much smaller order effect than 2022 GPT-3-era results, requiring larger samples to detect it reliably.

ideas.title: How Many Votes Is Enough? The Self-Consistency Cost Curve
ideas.question: When do extra votes stop improving an AI answer?
ideas.hook: Run self-consistency (sample-k-and-majority-vote) at k = 1,2,4,8,16,32 on a fixed reasoning benchmark with 2-3 cheap models, plotting accuracy vs k against the linearly-growing token cost.
ideas.firstMonth: Week1: pick a fixed 40-item math/reasoning benchmark with exact-answer grading. Week2: build a sampling-and-voting harness with per-call cost logging. Week3: run the k-sweep x2 repeats per k on one model. Week4: first accuracy-vs-k and cost-vs-k plots.
ideas.experiment: Run self-consistency (sample-k-and-majority-vote) at k = 1,2,4,8,16,32 on a fixed reasoning benchmark with 2-3 cheap models, plotting accuracy vs k against the linearly-growing token cost. Surprising question: exactly where does the marginal accuracy gain per extra sample cross below the marginal cost, and does that crossover shift with model or task difficulty?
ideas.baseline: Exact-match grading on math/reasoning answers with known solutions; majority vote is a deterministic function of the logged samples.
ideas.publicationPath: Extend to 3 models x difficulty-stratified items to derive a practical 'stop sampling here' rule for cost-aware agent deployments. Target: NeurIPS D&B workshop or a cost-aware-inference workshop.
ideas.risk: Budget can balloon quickly at k=32 across many items; needs careful item-subsetting and a hard cost cap.
ideas.pivot: Use the first month to test whether the proposed comparison is feasible and distinct from earlier work; discuss scope changes with a mentor.
ideas.resources: ~¥500 API credits (sampling multiplies call count), laptop.

ideas.title: Wrong Answer or Wrong Grader? Auditing Exact-Match Brittleness
ideas.question: How often does a strict grader reject an answer that is actually right?
ideas.hook: Take the transcripts a standard exact-match/regex grader marks 'incorrect' on a benchmark and dual-code a stratified sample by hand to classify each as truly-wrong vs correctly-reasoned-but-differently-formatted (units, rounding, phrasing).
ideas.firstMonth: Week1: run a fixed 60-item numeric/short-answer benchmark on one model and collect the exact-match 'wrong' subset. Week2: build a stricter/looser grader variant (numeric tolerance, unit normalization). Week3: dual-code a 100-item stratified sample for true-wrong vs format-mismatch, computing inter-rater agreement (manual vs LLM-judge re-grading). Week4: false-negative-rate table by model and format type.
ideas.experiment: Take the transcripts a standard exact-match/regex grader marks 'incorrect' on a benchmark and dual-code a stratified sample by hand to classify each as truly-wrong vs correctly-reasoned-but-differently-formatted (units, rounding, phrasing). Surprising question: what fraction of 'failures' on cheap CN-provider models are actually grading-script false negatives, and does that fraction differ by model or answer-format type?
ideas.baseline: Dual-coded manual plus rule-based re-grading with a documented inter-rater agreement (Cohen's kappa) as the objectivity check.
ideas.publicationPath: Extend across 3 benchmarks and release an open-source 'grading-robustness checker' that flags likely false negatives for any exact-match benchmark. Target: NeurIPS D&B workshop or an EMNLP evaluation-methods track.
ideas.risk: Manual re-coding is labor-intensive and can be subjective; needs a fixed rubric and a reported inter-rater agreement score to stay objective.
ideas.pivot: Use the first month to test whether the proposed comparison is feasible and distinct from earlier work; discuss scope changes with a mentor.
ideas.resources: Free/near-free (small API use), laptop.

ideas.title: Matched-Compute Replication Audit of a Published Agent Benchmark Claim
ideas.question: Does a published agent improvement survive a fair replication?
ideas.hook: Pick one recent, compute-light published claim about agent accuracy (a harness/prompting trick reported to boost a public benchmark by X points) and attempt a matched-compute replication using only cheap CN-provider APIs, reporting the…
ideas.firstMonth: Week1: survey 3-5 candidate papers with a small, exactly-specified benchmark and a clear reported delta; pick one with fully open materials. Week2: reimplement the baseline and the proposed technique on a cheap model. Week3: run both conditions with enough repeats (borrowing D01-01's run-count method) to get a CI on the delta. Week4: first side-by-side plot of claimed delta vs replicated delta with CI.

ideas.title: Fault-injection Lyapunov exponent for tool-using agents
ideas.question: How does one bad tool result spread through an agent's later actions?
ideas.hook: Wrap a cheap-LLM function-calling agent so one corrupted tool result (flipped sign, truncated string, wrong file) can be injected at a chosen step, then measure how fast the agent's trajectory diverges from a clean re-run using a…
ideas.firstMonth: Week 1: wrap one cheap LLM API with 3 toy tools (calculator, file-read, mock search) in a ~200-line harness (mentor-provided skeleton); log full transcripts as JSON. Week 2: run 5 fixed multi-step tasks with no corruption and define a task-state distance metric between two transcripts. Week 3: inject one corrupted tool output at step k (k=1..5) across the 5 tasks; plot distance-from-clean vs. steps-since-injection. Week 4: fit a per-corruption-type growth rate ('local Lyapunov exponent') and produce the first divergence-curve plot.
ideas.experiment: Wrap a cheap-LLM function-calling agent so one corrupted tool result (flipped sign, truncated string, wrong file) can be injected at a chosen step, then measure how fast the agent's trajectory diverges from a clean re-run using a task-state distance metric. The surprising question: does divergence grow like a clean exponential ('chaotic') or saturate ('self-correcting'), and does the growth rate depend more on corruption type than on model size?
ideas.baseline: Task-state distance to a deterministic clean-run trajectory (and match to a known-correct final answer) is machine-computed, not judged; recovery = final answer matches ground truth despite the injected fault.
ideas.publicationPath: 12-month result: a taxonomy of tool-corruption types (numeric noise, truncation, wrong-file swap, adversarial text) each with a measured divergence exponent and recovery-basin size across 3-4 cheap LLMs and 2 harness designs (with/without a self-check step); empirical measurement paper targeting a NeurIPS/ICLR agent-safety workshop or a D&B-track submission.
ideas.risk: Designing a good task-state distance metric is fiddly and mentor-dependent; a bad metric yields noisy, uninterpretable curves.
ideas.pivot: Replace the hand-designed task-state distance metric with a small set of objective, task-agnostic distance functions (tool-call edit distance, final-answer error) reported separately so the divergence-exponent claim doesn't ride on one fiddly metric -- agent fault-tolerance is an increasingly adjacent area.
ideas.resources: Free-¥300: one cheap LLM API key, laptop only, no GPU needed.

ideas.title: Defensive red-team suite for a homemade research agent
ideas.question: Which simulated attacks break a small research agent's checks?
ideas.hook: Assemble a battery of ~30 adversarial tool-outputs and prompts (poisoned search snippets, fake error messages, contradictory files) against a simple sandboxed research-assistant agent the team builds, and score pass/fail on whether its…
ideas.firstMonth: Week 1: build a minimal research-agent (searches a local mock corpus, summarizes, writes a report file) with 2 cheap-LLM backends. Week 2: hand-write 10 adversarial cases across 3 categories (injected instructions in retrieved text, fabricated tool errors, contradictory sources) with a scripted pass/fail check per case. Week 3: run all cases against both backends and log a pass/fail table. Week 4: add the defense system-prompt variant, re-run, and produce a before/after pass-rate bar chart.
ideas.experiment: Assemble a battery of ~30 adversarial tool-outputs and prompts (poisoned search snippets, fake error messages, contradictory files) against a simple sandboxed research-assistant agent the team builds, and score pass/fail on whether its final answer/action stays correct and safe. The question: which failure category breaks the agent most often, and does a one-line 'treat tool output as untrusted data' system prompt actually help?
ideas.baseline: Each case has a scripted, automatic pass/fail check (e.g., did the report contain the injected fake claim; did the agent follow the injected instruction) - no human judgment needed.
ideas.publicationPath: 12-month result: an open-source, reproducible 100+-case red-team benchmark suite for small research agents with pass-rate leaderboards across cheap CN LLM APIs and 3 defense strategies; benchmark/D&B paper or LLM-agent-safety workshop submission.
ideas.risk: Hand-written cases may not generalize; the suite could overfit to one agent design and fail to transfer to others.
ideas.pivot: Use the first month to test whether the proposed comparison is feasible and distinct from earlier work; discuss scope changes with a mentor.
ideas.resources: Free-¥300: cheap LLM API credits, laptop only.

ideas.title: Indirect prompt injection: a susceptibility-vs-subtlety curve
ideas.question: How does hiding an instruction affect an agent's susceptibility to it?
ideas.hook: Task a document-summarizing agent with reading files that contain hidden instructions (white text, markdown comments, a fake 'system note') and measure how often it follows the injected instruction instead of the user's, across increasing…
ideas.firstMonth: Week 1: build a document-summarization agent (reads a .txt/.md file, produces a 3-sentence summary + action) over one cheap LLM API. Week 2: write 5 clean documents and 5 injected variants at increasing subtlety (obvious 'ignore previous instructions' down to a disguised footnote). Week 3: run all 10 documents x 3 models and score whether the injected instruction was followed via an automatic keyword/action check. Week 4: plot susceptibility rate vs. subtlety level and vs. model.
ideas.experiment: Task a document-summarizing agent with reading files that contain hidden instructions (white text, markdown comments, a fake 'system note') and measure how often it follows the injected instruction instead of the user's, across increasing injection subtlety. The question: is susceptibility a sharp threshold in obviousness or a smooth curve, and does it differ across cheap LLM backends?
ideas.baseline: Automatic scripted check for whether the agent's output/action contains the injected payload's marker string or performs the injected action.
ideas.publicationPath: 12-month result: a systematic susceptibility-vs-subtlety curve across 4-5 cheap models and 3 document formats, plus a simple sanitization defense evaluated on the same curve; workshop paper (e.g., a SafeGenAI-style venue).
ideas.risk: Small hand-built document set may not capture real-world injection diversity; must stay strictly defensive/measurement-only on the team's own sandboxed agent, never a real third-party site.
ideas.pivot: Use the first month to test whether the proposed comparison is feasible and distinct from earlier work; discuss scope changes with a mentor.

ideas.title: Memory poisoning: how long does one false fact survive?
ideas.question: How long does a false fact survive in an agent's memory?
ideas.hook: Give a note-taking agent a persistent memory file it reads/writes across sessions, seed one false fact mid-session, and measure over how many subsequent turns the false fact keeps corrupting the agent's decisions before it is overwritten…
ideas.firstMonth: Week 1: build a minimal agent with a JSON memory file updated after each turn across a 10-turn synthetic task. Week 2: script 5 poisoning injection points (early/mid/late) with one false fact each; define an automatic check for whether downstream answers use the false fact. Week 3: measure persistence length (turns until the fact stops being used) with no defense. Week 4: add a simple periodic audit step and re-measure persistence and cost overhead.
ideas.experiment: Give a note-taking agent a persistent memory file it reads/writes across sessions, seed one false fact mid-session, and measure over how many subsequent turns the false fact keeps corrupting the agent's decisions before it is overwritten or caught. The question: does a periodic 'fact-audit' pass reliably clear poisoned entries, and at what token/API cost?
ideas.baseline: Scripted check on whether a downstream agent answer/action matches the true vs. poisoned fact - deterministic string/value comparison.
ideas.publicationPath: 12-month result: a persistence-vs-defense-cost curve across injection timing, memory-file size, and 2-3 audit strategies, plus a taxonomy of which fact types (numeric vs. preference vs. instruction) persist longest; workshop paper on agent memory safety.
ideas.risk: Automatically detecting 'downstream use of the fact' gets harder once tasks are open-ended; may need to restrict to structured-answer tasks.
ideas.pivot: Use the first month to test whether the proposed comparison is feasible and distinct from earlier work; discuss scope changes with a mentor.

ideas.question: When does confident but incorrect feedback make an agent abandon a right answer?
ideas.hook: Give an agent a battery of arithmetic/logic questions it answers correctly, then script a fake 'user' pushback with a confidently wrong correction, and measure the flip rate across model, question difficulty, and pushback phrasing (polite…
ideas.firstMonth: Week 1: assemble 30 objectively-checkable questions (arithmetic, unit conversion, simple logic) with known answers. ideas.title: Long-horizon drift: is there a turn-count collapse threshold?
ideas.question: Does an agent lose track of its goal suddenly or gradually over a long task?
ideas.hook: Run a single agent on a long (50-200 step) multi-tool task with no injected faults at all, just ordinary context growth, and track a goal-fidelity score every few turns to see whether performance decays smoothly or drops sharply past some…
ideas.firstMonth: Week 1: build a long-horizon toy task (maintain and update a structured inventory file over many scripted sub-tasks) runnable for 50+ turns on a cheap API. Week 2: define a goal-fidelity metric computable at any turn (fraction of inventory fields still correct vs. ground truth). Week 3: run 3 context-management strategies (full history, sliding window, periodic summarization) for 50 turns each, logging fidelity every 5 turns. Week 4: produce fidelity-vs-turn curves for all 3 strategies and identify any collapse point.
ideas.experiment: Run a single agent on a long (50-200 step) multi-tool task with no injected faults at all, just ordinary context growth, and track a goal-fidelity score every few turns to see whether performance decays smoothly or drops sharply past some turn count. ideas.baseline: Ground-truth inventory state is fully known/simulated by the harness at every turn, so fidelity is an exact numeric comparison, never judged.
ideas.publicationPath: 12-month result: fidelity-vs-turn-count curves across 3-4 context strategies and 2-3 model context-window sizes, framed as a finite-size-scaling-style analysis, with a proposed early-warning fidelity metric; target a PRE/PR-Research-class or NeurIPS agents-workshop paper - the scaling-law framing is the junior's stretch goal.
ideas.risk: Ambitious scope - the scaling-law framing may not pan out (decay could be smooth, no sharp transition); the fidelity-curve dataset is still a solid fallback rung.

ideas.title: Error amplification vs. tool-chain depth
ideas.question: How does adding more tool steps change the effect of an early error?
ideas.hook: Chain N sequential tool calls (extract -> transform -> compute -> format -> write) with a single injected wrong intermediate value at a fixed position, and measure what fraction of the final output is wrong as a function of chain length N…
ideas.firstMonth: Week 1: build a 5-step scripted tool pipeline over one cheap LLM API where each step's output feeds the next. Week 2: define an automatic 'fraction correct' metric for the final output vs. ground truth. Week 3: inject one wrong intermediate value at each of the 5 positions and measure the final-output error rate per injection position. Week 4: extend the chain to N=10 and N=15, add an optional self-check step every k links, and compare error rates with/without checkpoints.
ideas.experiment: Chain N sequential tool calls (extract -> transform -> compute -> format -> write) with a single injected wrong intermediate value at a fixed position, and measure what fraction of the final output is wrong as a function of chain length N and checkpoint frequency. The question: does error amplification grow linearly with depth, or does a cheap self-consistency checkpoint every k steps cut it superlinearly?
ideas.baseline: Every pipeline step has an exactly computable correct intermediate/final value (arithmetic/string transforms), so correctness is machine-checked end to end.
ideas.publicationPath: 12-month result: an error-amplification-vs-depth curve (with and without checkpointing) across 3-4 chain lengths and 2-3 cheap models, plus a cost-benefit analysis of checkpoint frequency (accuracy gained per extra API call); short paper or workshop submission.
ideas.risk: Toy pipelines may be too clean; needs realistic-feeling tool steps (not pure math) to keep the failure mode representative of real agent chains.
ideas.pivot: Use the first month to test whether the proposed comparison is feasible and distinct from earlier work; discuss scope changes with a mentor.

ideas.title: The boiling frog: detection threshold for gradual tool-output drift
ideas.question: When does an agent notice a tool that slowly becomes inaccurate?
ideas.hook: Instead of one abrupt corruption, gradually drift a mock tool's numeric outputs by a slowly growing bias and measure the drift magnitude at which downstream answers first become measurably wrong, separately from the magnitude at which the…
ideas.firstMonth: Week 1: build a mock tool that returns a value with a controllable, slowly increasing bias (0% to 50% over a run). Week 2: script a fixed downstream task consuming the tool's value and define an automatic correctness check. Week 3: run the drift schedule, logging at each step whether the final answer is correct and whether the agent's text flags any anomaly (keyword-based detector). Week 4: plot both thresholds (correctness-breaks vs. anomaly-flagged) on the same drift-magnitude axis.
ideas.experiment: Instead of one abrupt corruption, gradually drift a mock tool's numeric outputs by a slowly growing bias and measure the drift magnitude at which downstream answers first become measurably wrong, separately from the magnitude at which the agent ever remarks that 'something seems off.' The question: is the silent-failure gap large - does the agent give wrong answers long before it notices anything strange?
ideas.baseline: The simulated drift and correct task answers give an exact task-error threshold. The first warning is measured with an operational detector whose relation to anomaly recognition requires validation; it is not an exact measure of awareness.
ideas.publicationPath: 12-month result: a systematic 'silent failure gap' measurement (correctness-break threshold vs. self-reported-anomaly threshold) across drift rates, task types, and 3-4 models, benchmarked against an off-the-shelf detector as an upper bound; workshop paper on agent reliability/monitoring.
ideas.risk: Keyword-based 'did the agent notice' detector is a crude proxy for genuine anomaly awareness; needs manual spot-checks to validate. A detector for prompt injection is not automatically a suitable or upper-bound baseline for numeric drift.
ideas.pivot: Swap the keyword-based 'did it notice' detector for a quantitative signal derived from the agent's own token-level confidence/logprob shift, addressing the reviewer's 'crude proxy' critique while keeping the gradual-drift twist that abrupt-injection defenses like UniGuardian don't cover.
ideas.resources: Free-¥200: cheap LLM API, laptop only.

ideas.title: Cost-of-resilience: a fault-recovery vs. API-price Pareto frontier
ideas.question: How much does reliable fault recovery cost?
ideas.hook: Reuse a fault-injection harness (one corrupted tool result per run) across 4-5 cheap CN/US LLM APIs of very different prices, measuring both post-fault task correctness and total API cost in yuan to build a resilience-per-yuan Pareto…
ideas.firstMonth: Week 1: reuse/build a small fault-injection harness (one corrupted tool result per run) over a fixed 10-task suite. Week 2: wire in 3 cheap CN APIs (DeepSeek/Qwen/GLM) with per-call cost tracking. Week 3: run the full suite x each model, logging recovery rate and yuan spent. Week 4: add a 'self-check before finalizing' prompt variant for each model, re-run, and plot recovery-rate vs. cost for all model x prompt-variant combinations.
ideas.experiment: Reuse a fault-injection harness (one corrupted tool result per run) across 4-5 cheap CN/US LLM APIs of very different prices, measuring both post-fault task correctness and total API cost in yuan to build a resilience-per-yuan Pareto frontier. The question: does paying more actually buy meaningfully better fault recovery, or does a cheap model with a simple self-check prompt dominate an expensive model without one?
ideas.baseline: Recovery rate is the fraction of the suite where the post-fault final answer matches the known-correct answer; cost is metered API billing - both exact, no judgment calls.
ideas.publicationPath: 12-month result: a resilience-per-yuan Pareto frontier across 5+ models and 2-3 defense prompt strategies, with a recommended 'best cheap recipe' for a fault-tolerant lab research agent; short empirical paper or workshop submission useful to cost-conscious agent builders.
ideas.risk: Price lists for cheap CN APIs change quickly; yuan-cost numbers need an 'as of' date and re-measurement before any write-up.
ideas.pivot: Use the first month to test whether the proposed comparison is feasible and distinct from earlier work; discuss scope changes with a mentor.

ideas.title: In-context vaccination: does a few-shot injection warning help?
ideas.question: Can warning examples help an agent resist injected instructions?
ideas.hook: Compare a zero-cost defense (a few in-context examples of injection attempts and correct refusals added to the system prompt) against a state-of-the-art optimized injection attack, measuring success rate versus a heavier dedicated…
ideas.firstMonth: Week 1: build (or reuse from D02-03) a document-reading agent with a baseline, no-defense system prompt. ideas.title: Two-agent equality game: LLM message bits vs the Shannon minimum
ideas.question: How many message bits do two agents need to check whether their strings match?
ideas.hook: Two LLM agents each privately hold an n-bit string and must decide, via a handful of short text messages, whether the strings are equal; measure the empirical bit-cost of their exchanged tokens against the classical…
ideas.firstMonth: Implement the EQUALITY function (two random n-bit strings, n=4..16) as an API-mediated two-agent protocol; log every exchanged message, estimate its bit content, and by week 4 plot empirical bits/round vs n against the Theta(n) deterministic and O(log n) randomized bounds.
ideas.experiment: Two LLM agents each privately hold an n-bit string and must decide, via a handful of short text messages, whether the strings are equal; measure the empirical bit-cost of their exchanged tokens against the classical communication-complexity lower bound (deterministic Theta(n), randomized O(log n)). Surprising question: does LLM message length track the theoretical bit bound, or do agents waste tokens on natural-language scaffolding that inflates cost by orders of magnitude?
ideas.baseline: Deterministic/randomized communication-complexity lower bounds for equality and set-disjointness are textbook results (Yao's framework); correctness of the equal/not-equal decision is trivially checked against ground truth.
ideas.publicationPath: A systematic study of token efficiency across several classic two-party communication problems (equality, set-disjointness, greater-than) and multiple LLM backends, quantifying the natural-language communication-complexity overhead; targets an AAMAS short paper or a COLM/ICLR workshop.
ideas.risk: Converting free-form text to a fair 'bits' measure is subjective; mitigate by capping message length and reporting both raw token count and an entropy-coded estimate.
ideas.pivot: Use the first month to test whether the proposed comparison is feasible and distinct from earlier work; discuss scope changes with a mentor.
ideas.resources: laptop, cheap API calls (~¥100/month), no GPU

ideas.title: LLM public-goods game: contributions vs Nash zero and social optimum
ideas.question: How much do AI agents contribute to a shared public good?
ideas.hook: Run a repeated N-player public-goods game among LLM agents (each round: contribute part of an endowment to a shared, multiplied, evenly-split pot) and track contribution trajectories against the Nash prediction (zero, without punishment)…
ideas.firstMonth: Implement the standard linear public-goods game (multiplier 1<m<N) with 4-6 LLM agents over 10-20 rounds, no punishment; by week 4 produce the average-contribution-vs-round decay curve and overlay the Fehr-Gachter human baseline plus the Nash/social-optimum lines.
ideas.experiment: Run a repeated N-player public-goods game among LLM agents (each round: contribute part of an endowment to a shared, multiplied, evenly-split pot) and track contribution trajectories against the Nash prediction (zero, without punishment) and the social optimum (full contribution). Surprising question: do LLM-agent groups decay toward free-riding like classic human experiments, or do certain personas/model families sustain cooperation well above Nash?
ideas.baseline: Nash equilibrium (zero contribution, no punishment) and the Pareto/social optimum (full contribution) are exact closed-form predictions of the linear public-goods game, so every deviation is precisely quantifiable.
ideas.publicationPath: A comparative study across model families, temperatures, and persona prompts of cooperation trajectories in public-goods and related social-dilemma games, extended with a punishment mechanism; targets a behavioral-game-theory venue (Games, PLOS ONE) or an AAMAS/COLM workshop.
ideas.risk: Results may be highly prompt-sensitive (framing effects); mitigate with a fixed, pre-registered set of prompt templates and multiple random seeds.
ideas.pivot: Use the first month to test whether the proposed comparison is feasible and distinct from earlier work; discuss scope changes with a mentor.

ideas.title: Does an LLM jury follow the Condorcet jury theorem?
ideas.question: When does a group of AI voters become more accurate than one voter?
ideas.hook: Have K independent LLM agents each answer the same factual question (with per-agent accuracy p measured on a held-out set) and take a majority vote; measure how ensemble accuracy scales with K against the closed-form Condorcet Jury…
ideas.firstMonth: Pick a factual benchmark (trivia or arithmetic, known answers); measure single-agent accuracy p, then query K=1,3,5,...,15 independent agents (varied via temperature/persona) per question and majority-vote; by week 4 plot empirical ensemble accuracy vs K against the Condorcet prediction from measured p.
ideas.experiment: Have K independent LLM agents each answer the same factual question (with per-agent accuracy p measured on a held-out set) and take a majority vote; measure how ensemble accuracy scales with K against the closed-form Condorcet Jury Theorem curve. Surprising question: do correlated LLM errors make the ensemble curve saturate far below the independent-voter prediction, and if so, at what K does adding more agents stop helping?
ideas.baseline: The Condorcet Jury Theorem gives an exact closed-form majority-vote accuracy formula from p and K; ground-truth question answers make every accuracy measurement exact rather than judged.
ideas.publicationPath: A quantitative study of the 'correlation gap' between the Condorcet prediction and real LLM-ensemble accuracy across question difficulty and model diversity (mixing model families to reduce correlation), targeting a COLM/EMNLP-findings-style short empirical paper.
ideas.risk: The theorem's independence assumption is likely violated by shared model biases; the main finding may be exactly this violation, which is a valid pre-committed outcome either way.
ideas.pivot: The reviewer's scoop claim checks out: 'More Agents' already measures ensemble-accuracy-vs-K saturation from correlated LLM errors; salvage only the explicit closed-form Condorcet comparison plus deliberate cross-family model mixing to reduce correlation, citing the prior saturation result directly rather than re-deriving it as new.
ideas.resources: laptop, cheap API (~¥100-300/month depending on K and question count)

ideas.question: Which AI persona succeeds across repeated cooperation games?

ideas.firstMonth: Implement pairwise iterated Prisoner's Dilemma (200 rounds, noise-free) between 5 fixed strategies plus 1 free-form LLM persona; build the round-robin payoff matrix; by week 4 compute the tournament ranking and its replicator-dynamics fixed point.

ideas.title: LLM opinion dynamics: does bounded confidence predict cluster count?
ideas.question: Can a simple opinion model predict how AI agents form clusters?
ideas.hook: Place N LLM agents on a fixed social-network graph, each holding a scalar opinion it updates each round after seeing neighbors' opinions but only averaging with those inside its confidence radius epsilon (Hegselmann-Krause rule); measure…
ideas.firstMonth: Implement N=10-20 agents on a complete (or small random) graph with random initial opinions in [0,1]; hard-code the bounded-confidence filter in code with LLM agents supplying the reasoning wrapper for the updated value; by week 4 sweep epsilon and plot final cluster count against the known Hegselmann-Krause curve.
ideas.experiment: Place N LLM agents on a fixed social-network graph, each holding a scalar opinion it updates each round after seeing neighbors' opinions but only averaging with those inside its confidence radius epsilon (Hegselmann-Krause rule); measure the number of final opinion clusters vs epsilon against the known bounded-confidence phase diagram. Surprising question: does giving agents natural-language reasoning instead of pure numeric averaging shift the critical epsilon at which the population fragments?
ideas.baseline: The Hegselmann-Krause model's cluster-count-vs-epsilon relationship is an established, numerically reproducible opinion-dynamics result the empirical curve can be directly overlaid on.
ideas.publicationPath: A study contrasting a pure-numeric bounded-confidence simulation with an 'LLM-reasoned' version (agents can also change their mind for qualitative reasons) for systematic deviations from the classical phase diagram across network topologies; targets a complexity/network-science venue (Physica A, JASSS) or an LLM-agent workshop.
ideas.risk: LLM 'reasoning' may not respect a strict epsilon cutoff if only softly prompted; mitigate by hard-coding the confidence filter and using the LLM only to generate the value within the allowed neighbor set.
ideas.pivot: Use the first month to test whether the proposed comparison is feasible and distinct from earlier work; discuss scope changes with a mentor.
ideas.resources: laptop, cheap API (~¥150/month for the N x rounds x epsilon sweep)

ideas.title: LLM bargaining: does the split match the alternating-offers equilibrium?
ideas.question: Do bargaining agents reach the split predicted by game theory?
ideas.hook: Two LLM agents bargain over a fixed pie via alternating offers with a known per-round discount/deadline structure, and the resulting split is compared to the closed-form subgame-perfect equilibrium predicted by the alternating-offers…
ideas.firstMonth: Implement a fixed-pie alternating-offers protocol (pie shrinks by a known factor delta each round, or ends with known deadline probability) between two LLM agents with stated discount factors; run 20+ negotiations per delta value; by week 4 plot the empirical average split vs the closed-form equilibrium split as a function of delta.
ideas.experiment: Two LLM agents bargain over a fixed pie via alternating offers with a known per-round discount/deadline structure, and the resulting split is compared to the closed-form subgame-perfect equilibrium predicted by the alternating-offers bargaining model. Surprising question: do agents with asymmetric discount factors (one impatient, one patient) split the pie in proportion to theory, or does one model family systematically out-negotiate another regardless of its theoretical disadvantage?
ideas.baseline: The subgame-perfect equilibrium split of the alternating-offers bargaining game is an exact closed-form function of the discount factor(s), directly comparable to every negotiated split.
ideas.publicationPath: A cross-model-family negotiation study (does a strong model out-negotiate a cheap one; does persona/prompting shift bargaining power beyond what discount factors predict), with a multi-issue negotiation extension; targets an AAMAS paper or a negotiation-in-AI workshop.
ideas.risk: LLM agents may mis-track pie-shrinkage arithmetic over many rounds; mitigate by having the harness (not the LLM) compute and state the current pie size each round.
ideas.pivot: Use the first month to test whether the proposed comparison is feasible and distinct from earlier work; discuss scope changes with a mentor.
ideas.resources: laptop, cheap API (~¥150/month)

ideas.title: LLM Minority Game: does the volatility phase transition survive?
ideas.question: Does a group of AI agents reproduce the Minority Game's volatility transition?
ideas.hook: Have a population of LLM agents repeatedly choose between two rooms, rewarded for being in the minority (the classic Minority Game), and measure aggregate volatility (variance of the winning-side size) vs agents' memory/strategy-space…
ideas.firstMonth: Implement the classic Minority Game with N=51-101 agents using deterministic lookup-table strategies to reproduce the textbook phase transition as a validation rung; by week 4, swap LLM-agent decision-making into a small sub-population and compare aggregate volatility to the deterministic baseline at matched memory length m.
ideas.experiment: Have a population of LLM agents repeatedly choose between two rooms, rewarded for being in the minority (the classic Minority Game), and measure aggregate volatility (variance of the winning-side size) vs agents' memory/strategy-space size, comparing to the well-known statistical-mechanics phase transition between crowd-dominated and unpredictable regimes. Surprising question: does replacing hand-coded lookup-table strategies with free-form LLM reasoning shift, sharpen, or destroy the known phase transition?
ideas.baseline: The Minority Game's volatility-vs-alpha curve and phase transition are established, replica-method-solvable statistical-mechanics results; the deterministic-strategy rung gives an exact, checkable baseline before any LLM agents are introduced.
ideas.publicationPath: A full comparison of LLM-agent vs canonical strategy-table populations across the control parameter alpha=2^m/N, testing whether the crowd/anti-crowd statistical-mechanics phase transition (and its finite-size scaling) survives natural-language reasoning; targets PRE or J. Stat. Mech. This is the direction's most ambitious idea, giving the junior a full replicate-extend-novel research arc.
ideas.risk: Statistical-mechanics-quality phase-transition data (large N, many disorder realizations) is expensive with real LLM calls; the fail-soft ladder handles this since rung 1 (deterministic replication) needs no API budget at all.
ideas.pivot: LLM El Farol studies exist but are qualitative/spatial; the unclaimed result is the quantitative volatility-vs-alpha=2^m/N curve against the exact Minority Game transition (alpha_c~0.34), so make that scan with the deterministic strategy-table population as the calibrated baseline the whole paper. (Orchestrator web check, overrides batch A.)
ideas.resources: laptop for the deterministic baseline; ~¥500-1000/month API budget once LLM agents are added at larger N; no GPU required

ideas.title: Does LLM debate raise judge accuracy on ground-truth puzzles?
ideas.question: Does debate help an AI judge solve questions with known answers?
ideas.hook: Two LLM 'debater' agents argue opposite answers to a verifiable puzzle in front of a deliberately weaker 'judge' agent that only sees the debate transcript, not the raw problem; measure whether judge accuracy on the ground-truth answer is…
ideas.firstMonth: Assemble ~50 puzzles with exact known answers (logic-grid or verifiable arithmetic problems), solvable by a strong model but not always by a deliberately weaker judge model; implement judge-alone, single-advocate, and two-sided-debate conditions; by week 4 report judge accuracy in each condition on a held-out puzzle set.
ideas.experiment: Two LLM 'debater' agents argue opposite answers to a verifiable puzzle in front of a deliberately weaker 'judge' agent that only sees the debate transcript, not the raw problem; measure whether judge accuracy on the ground-truth answer is higher with two-sided debate than with a single unopposed advocate or the judge answering alone. Surprising question: does adversarial debate reliably help a weak judge converge on the truth, or can a persuasive-but-wrong debater systematically win?
ideas.baseline: Every puzzle has a single, mechanically checkable correct answer, so judge correctness is never a judgment call, unlike most debate-protocol studies that rely on human graders.
ideas.publicationPath: A systematic study across puzzle difficulty, debate-round count, and judge/debater strength gaps, characterizing when debate helps vs hurts truth-tracking; targets a COLM/NeurIPS workshop on scalable oversight.
ideas.risk: Puzzles must be hard enough for the weak judge alone but unambiguous enough to grade; start with off-the-shelf logic-puzzle generators to avoid hand-authoring bias.
ideas.pivot: Use the first month to test whether the proposed comparison is feasible and distinct from earlier work; discuss scope changes with a mentor.
ideas.resources: laptop, cheap API (~¥200/month; judge should be a cheaper/weaker model than the debaters)

ideas.title: First-price vs second-price: do LLM bidders shade like Bayes-Nash?
ideas.question: Do AI auction bidders adjust their bids as game theory predicts?

ideas.title: Easy-hard-easy curve for LLM reasoners at 3-SAT threshold
ideas.originalDirection: LLMs vs solvers: games, puzzles, combinatorial hardness
ideas.question: Where do randomly generated logic puzzles become hardest for AI reasoners?
ideas.hook: Generate random 3-SAT instances across clause-to-variable ratios and ask cheap-API LLMs (zero-shot and CoT) to decide satisfiability, scoring accuracy and token cost against an exact DPLL/CDCL solver.
ideas.firstMonth: Install python-sat (or write a small DPLL solver), generate 500 random 3-SAT instances at ratios 2-6 (20 vars), verify each with the solver, and run 50 instances through one LLM API zero-shot; plot accuracy vs ratio for a first hardness curve.
ideas.experiment: Generate random 3-SAT instances across clause-to-variable ratios and ask cheap-API LLMs (zero-shot and CoT) to decide satisfiability, scoring accuracy and token cost against an exact DPLL/CDCL solver. Does the classic easy-hard-easy computational-hardness curve reappear in LLM accuracy and reasoning-token length, and does it shift with model size or CoT budget?
ideas.baseline: Exact DPLL/CDCL solver output (SAT/UNSAT) plus the known theoretical satisfiability threshold for random 3-SAT.
ideas.publicationPath: Sweep ratio x model x prompting strategy (zero-shot/CoT/self-consistency) with token accounting, compare the empirical peak location/width to the known n=20-50 SAT threshold (~4.267), and fit a scaling law for reasoning-token cost near threshold; a math-AI or reasoning workshop paper (NeurIPS/ICLR/COLM) is plausible, PRE-style if framed as statistical mechanics of inference.
ideas.risk: Cheap LLM APIs may saturate at 100% or 0% accuracy outside a narrow ratio band; n must be chosen carefully to keep the transition inside an affordable, measurable range.
ideas.pivot: Use the first month to test whether the proposed comparison is feasible and distinct from earlier work; discuss scope changes with a mentor.
ideas.resources: Laptop only; ~¥100-300 in cheap-API credits (DeepSeek/Qwen) for a few hundred short prompts; no GPU needed.

ideas.title: k-coloring phase transition probed by LLM colorability calls
ideas.originalDirection: LLMs vs solvers: games, puzzles, combinatorial hardness
ideas.question: Can an AI recognize when a graph can be colored with a fixed number of colors?
ideas.hook: Generate random Erdos-Renyi graphs across mean degree near the known k-colorability threshold and ask an LLM to attempt a proper k-coloring, checked against an exact backtracking/SAT-based solver.
ideas.firstMonth: Physics half: generate G(n,p) graphs with networkx and compute mean degree; AI half: write an exact backtracking 3-colorability checker and a first LLM prompt loop; jointly plot LLM accuracy vs mean degree for k=3 on n=15-20 graphs.
ideas.experiment: Generate random Erdos-Renyi graphs across mean degree near the known k-colorability threshold and ask an LLM to attempt a proper k-coloring, checked against an exact backtracking/SAT-based solver. The physics student tunes the ensemble to the cavity-method-predicted threshold while the AI student runs the LLM harness; do LLM failure modes cluster at the same threshold as solver run-time, or elsewhere?
ideas.baseline: Exact backtracking/SAT-based coloring solver plus the known statistical-physics colorability threshold for random graphs.
ideas.publicationPath: Extend to k=3-5, compare threshold location/width against the belief-propagation-predicted colorability threshold, add a solver-augmented condition, and fit LLM-accuracy-transition width vs solver time-to-solution near threshold; target a physics-of-computation venue (PRE) or an ML+combinatorics workshop.
ideas.risk: Colorability-threshold sharpness depends on n; at the small n affordable for LLM prompting the transition may be too smeared to distinguish from noise.
ideas.pivot: Use the first month to test whether the proposed comparison is feasible and distinct from earlier work; discuss scope changes with a mentor.
ideas.resources: Laptop only; ~¥100-200 in API credits; networkx + a SAT library, no GPU.

ideas.title: Calibrating when an LLM agent should call a solver
ideas.originalDirection: LLMs vs solvers: games, puzzles, combinatorial hardness
ideas.question: When should an AI agent hand a problem to an exact solver?
ideas.hook: Build a single-agent harness with access to an exact solver tool (SAT/Sudoku) and measure, as instance hardness increases, whether the agent's decision to call the tool tracks an oracle policy that calls it exactly above the hardness…
ideas.firstMonth: Wrap an existing SAT solver as a callable Python tool; build a minimal loop where the LLM must decide call-or-not before attempting an instance itself; run on 100 instances spanning easy to hard and plot call-rate vs instance hardness for a first calibration curve.
ideas.experiment: Build a single-agent harness with access to an exact solver tool (SAT/Sudoku) and measure, as instance hardness increases, whether the agent's decision to call the tool tracks an oracle policy that calls it exactly above the hardness where self-solving fails. Is miscalibration (over- or under-calling) a predictable function of prompt framing and model confidence, i.e. can we plot an ROC-style curve for tool-use decisions?
ideas.baseline: Solver's verified answer gives own-solve accuracy per hardness bin; the 'should have called' label is derived directly from that measured accuracy.
ideas.publicationPath: Extend to Sudoku and Sokoban tools, add a cost-aware oracle (tool call has a token/latency cost), define and report an AUC-style calibration score across models/providers, and test whether few-shot calibration examples shift the curve; plausible at an agents/tool-use workshop (NeurIPS/ICLR), main-track shot if the calibration-metric framing proves novel.
ideas.risk: Defining a single 'hardness' scalar comparable across puzzle families (SAT ratio vs Sudoku givens) is non-trivial; start within one family before generalizing.
ideas.pivot: Use the first month to test whether the proposed comparison is feasible and distinct from earlier work; discuss scope changes with a mentor.
ideas.resources: Laptop only; ~¥200-400 in API credits for repeated tool-decision trials; no GPU.

ideas.firstMonth: Write a backtracking Sudoku solver with technique/backtrack counting, generate 100 puzzles spanning easy to expert, and run 30 through an LLM API zero-shot, logging correctness and token count against the solver's backtrack count.

ideas.title: Sokoban push-count optimality gap for LLM planners
ideas.originalDirection: LLMs vs solvers: games, puzzles, combinatorial hardness
ideas.question: How far are an AI's Sokoban solutions from the shortest possible solution?
ideas.hook: Ask an LLM to solve small Sokoban levels (as a text grid) and compare its move sequence to the exact minimum-push solution from a BFS/IDA* solver, measuring success rate and excess-move ratio as box count grows.
ideas.firstMonth: Write or reuse a small BFS/IDA* Sokoban solver for grids up to 3 boxes, generate 50 solvable levels, and run them through an LLM API with a text-grid prompt; plot success rate and excess-push ratio vs box count.
ideas.experiment: Ask an LLM to solve small Sokoban levels (as a text grid) and compare its move sequence to the exact minimum-push solution from a BFS/IDA* solver, measuring success rate and excess-move ratio as box count grows. ideas.title: Nim and Sprague-Grundy: does the LLM find the XOR rule
ideas.originalDirection: LLMs vs solvers: games, puzzles, combinatorial hardness
ideas.question: Does an AI learn Nim's XOR rule or repeat a familiar strategy?
ideas.hook: Play an LLM against an exact Sprague-Grundy-optimal opponent across single-pile Nim, multi-pile Nim, and Wythoff's game, measuring win rate and whether the LLM's stated reasoning ever recovers the XOR/Grundy-value invariant.
ideas.firstMonth: Implement exact optimal Nim play (XOR rule) and a game loop where the LLM plays first-mover across 2-4 piles with small pile sizes; run 100 games per pile-count and plot LLM win rate vs pile count against the known optimal baseline.
ideas.experiment: Play an LLM against an exact Sprague-Grundy-optimal opponent across single-pile Nim, multi-pile Nim, and Wythoff's game, measuring win rate and whether the LLM's stated reasoning ever recovers the XOR/Grundy-value invariant. Does win rate degrade smoothly with pile count (deeper search), or does the LLM either 'get' the invariant or not?
ideas.baseline: Exact Sprague-Grundy theory gives optimal play and win/loss status for every position.
ideas.publicationPath: Extend to Wythoff's game and a misere-Nim variant, probe whether few-shot XOR-rule examples change the win-rate curve, and test transfer to a novel isomorphic game (same Grundy structure, different surface story) to distinguish learned invariant from memorization; a game-theoretic AI reasoning workshop paper is plausible.
ideas.risk: LLMs may have memorized textbook Nim strategy from pretraining, so a positive result could reflect memorization; the isomorphic-game transfer test is essential to rule this out.
ideas.pivot: Build the whole paper around the isomorphic-game transfer test (same Grundy structure, different surface story), the one piece the well-trodden 'LLM plays a classic combinatorial game' genre hasn't isolated cleanly, rather than the raw win-rate-vs-pile-count curve.
ideas.resources: Laptop only; ~¥50-150 in API credits for game-play trials; no GPU.

ideas.title: Wordle: how many bits does the LLM leave on the table
ideas.originalDirection: LLMs vs solvers: games, puzzles, combinatorial hardness
ideas.question: How much useful information does an AI leave unused in Wordle?
ideas.hook: Build an entropy-maximizing (near-optimal) Wordle solver as an oracle, then measure the bit-gap between an LLM's guesses and the optimal guess at each turn across many games.
ideas.firstMonth: Implement a Wordle simulator with the official word list and a greedy entropy-maximizing solver; run an LLM through 50 games via API, logging each guess and the entropy it achieved versus the optimal choice; plot per-turn bit-gap.
ideas.experiment: Build an entropy-maximizing (near-optimal) Wordle solver as an oracle, then measure the bit-gap between an LLM's guesses and the optimal guess at each turn across many games. Is the gap roughly constant per turn, or does it spike specifically when the LLM must reason about the disjoint case where its favorite guess cannot be the answer?
ideas.baseline: Entropy-optimal solver gives the maximum expected information gain per turn, an exact information-theoretic ceiling.
ideas.publicationPath: Test multiple models/providers and prompting styles (with/without shown entropy hints), characterize when the bit-gap spikes (early guesses vs endgame), and compare against a POMDP-optimal ceiling; a fun, accessible reasoning-under-uncertainty workshop paper, or an AJP-style note on information theory in a familiar game.
ideas.risk: Popular LLMs may have memorized known-optimal Wordle openers from training data, inflating early-guess performance independent of genuine reasoning; use a held-out custom word list to control for this.
ideas.pivot: Narrow the paper entirely to the turn-by-turn bit-gap curve and the disjoint-case reasoning spike, not general Wordle-playing ability, with a held-out/generated word list to defeat memorized-opener confounds -- the one angle the well-trodden LLM-plays-Wordle genre hasn't isolated cleanly.
ideas.resources: Laptop only; ~¥50-150 in API credits; no GPU.

ideas.title: A universal reasoning-token scaling law across solver-verified puzzles
ideas.originalDirection: LLMs vs solvers: games, puzzles, combinatorial hardness
ideas.question: Does the reasoning budget needed for accuracy scale similarly across puzzles?
ideas.hook: Collect solver-verified hardness and LLM reasoning-token counts across several puzzle families already running in this direction (3-SAT ratio, Sudoku backtracks, Sokoban box count, graph-coloring mean degree) and test whether a single…
ideas.firstMonth: Take the already-logged (token count, solver-difficulty) pairs from two puzzle families the group has running (e.g. 3-SAT and Sudoku), normalize each family's difficulty axis by its own solver search-tree-size proxy, and plot both on one token-cost-vs-normalized-difficulty axis to see if they collapse.
ideas.experiment: Collect solver-verified hardness and LLM reasoning-token counts across several puzzle families already running in this direction (3-SAT ratio, Sudoku backtracks, Sokoban box count, graph-coloring mean degree) and test whether a single scaling form fits across families, echoing the RL-trained-reasoner finding that token length is itself an optimized quantity. Is 'reasoning length' a universal currency of difficulty across combinatorial domains, or family-specific?
ideas.baseline: Each family's exact solver gives a machine-checkable difficulty proxy (search-tree size/backtrack count); token counts are exact API-reported counts.
ideas.publicationPath: Add 2 more families (Sokoban, coloring), fit and cross-validate a single scaling law, and test whether the collapse holds across model families/providers (DeepSeek/Qwen/GLM/Kimi) or is model-specific; a genuine cross-domain collapse would be a strong result for a reasoning-focused ML venue (ICLR/NeurIPS workshop, main-track if robust and surprising).
ideas.risk: Depends on other sub-teams' puzzle harnesses being built and logged with a consistent token/difficulty schema, so it needs early cross-team coordination on data format in week 1.
