ideas.title: Fair SA-vs-SB time-to-solution race, agent-tuned
ideas.question: Which optimizer wins when tuning and runtime budgets are matched?
ideas.hook: Build a common time-to-solution (TTS) benchmark harness that runs simulated annealing (SA) and simulated bifurcation (SB) on the same Max-Cut/Ising instances, with a cheap LLM agent proposing and testing hyperparameters (schedule shape,…
ideas.firstMonth: Week1: 2D Ising Metropolis + SA on small Max-Cut instances. Week2: wire up a TTS metric (runs to reach 99% success vs known optimum). Week3: implement the discrete SB update rule and reproduce a published small-instance result. Week4: script an LLM-agent loop that reads TTS logs and proposes the next hyperparameter setting for each solver.
ideas.experiment: Build a common time-to-solution (TTS) benchmark harness that runs simulated annealing (SA) and simulated bifurcation (SB) on the same Max-Cut/Ising instances, with a cheap LLM agent proposing and testing hyperparameters (schedule shape, SB timestep/pump ramp) from run logs. The question: does honest, agent-driven hyperparameter search change which algorithm 'wins,' or is the standard SA-loses-to-SB folklore robust to a fair tuning budget?
ideas.baseline: TTS and success probability measured against brute-force or published best-known solutions on benchmark instances — an objective, machine-checkable metric.
ideas.publicationPath: Extend to a systematic instance-family benchmark with agent-in-the-loop tuning vs grid-search baselines, reporting whether tuning method changes the SA/SB ranking; workshop paper at a combinatorial-optimization/AI4science venue, or a PRE methods note if scaling exponents are rigorously extracted (9-12 months).
ideas.risk: Correctly implementing SB's stiff ODE update is nontrivial for a first month; mitigated by SA-only as the guaranteed fail-soft rung 1.
ideas.pivot: No paper applies agent-driven tuning specifically to the SA-vs-SB folklore; pre-register both algorithms' search spaces and a shared compute budget before running either so the fairness claim itself is the airtight contribution, not just another benchmark.
ideas.resources: laptop only; cheap LLM API calls for the tuning agent, roughly ¥200/month.

ideas.title: Critical slowing down sets Ising annealing schedule limits
ideas.question: How does critical slowing down limit an Ising annealing schedule?
ideas.hook: Measure the dynamical critical exponent z of single-spin-flip Metropolis dynamics in the 2D Ising model from autocorrelation-time finite-size scaling near Tc, then test whether z predicts the residual-defect density left by a…
ideas.firstMonth: Week1: implement 2D Ising Metropolis, plot M(T) near Tc. Week2: measure autocorrelation time tau(T,L) for several lattice sizes. Week3: extract z from tau ~ L^z finite-size scaling. Week4: run linear-schedule SA sweeps through Tc and measure defect density vs schedule speed, compare to the KZ power law.
ideas.experiment: Measure the dynamical critical exponent z of single-spin-flip Metropolis dynamics in the 2D Ising model from autocorrelation-time finite-size scaling near Tc, then test whether z predicts the residual-defect density left by a linear-schedule simulated anneal through the critical point. The surprising question: does a purely classical, thermal anneal obey a Kibble-Zurek-style scaling law usually discussed only for quantum annealers?
ideas.baseline: 2D Ising has an exactly known Tc and universality class; autocorrelation time and defect density are directly computed, objective quantities.
ideas.publicationPath: Extend to compare z (and hence KZ exponents) across local update rules (checkerboard-parallel Metropolis, heat-bath, Glauber) to derive a schedule-design rule for SA-based Ising solvers; small PRE/AJP-class paper or workshop note.
ideas.risk: Clean power-law extraction for z needs more statistics/larger L than a laptop easily gives in month 1; mitigated by checking against the known literature value z≈2.17 as a sanity target.
ideas.pivot: Use the first month to test whether the proposed comparison is feasible and distinct from earlier work; discuss scope changes with a mentor.
ideas.resources: laptop only, free.

ideas.title: Avalanche size distribution in simulated annealing quenches
ideas.question: Do simulated-annealing quenches produce characteristic avalanche statistics?
ideas.hook: Log every downhill spin-flip's energy drop during a simulated-annealing quench of a 2D random-bond Ising spin glass, bin consecutive flips into avalanches, and test whether the avalanche-size distribution is power-law and how its cutoff…
ideas.firstMonth: Week1: implement 2D +/-J spin-glass SA. Week2: instrument the code to log energy-drop event sizes during a quench. Week3: build avalanche-size histograms and test for power-law scaling (MLE + KS test). Week4: vary quench rate and measure how the largest avalanche size scales.
ideas.experiment: Log every downhill spin-flip's energy drop during a simulated-annealing quench of a 2D random-bond Ising spin glass, bin consecutive flips into avalanches, and test whether the avalanche-size distribution is power-law and how its cutoff scales with quench rate. This ports avalanche/self-organized-criticality analysis, familiar from disordered magnets and memcomputing solvers, onto the workhorse SA algorithm itself.
ideas.baseline: Energy is exactly computable at every Monte Carlo step; power-law fits are tested with standard, objective statistical methods (MLE, KS test).
ideas.publicationPath: Compare avalanche statistics across solvers (SA vs digital memcomputing vs SB) on the same instances to test whether a solver's avalanche exponent predicts its TTS performance; PRE-class paper.
ideas.risk: Finite-size/finite-statistics effects can mimic power laws; mitigated by rigorous MLE+KS fitting rather than eyeballing log-log plots.
ideas.pivot: Equilibrium spin-glass avalanches and SOC-based optimizers are known; keep the claim on the cross-solver comparison (SA vs simulated bifurcation vs memcomputing) of avalanche exponents and whether they predict time-to-solution. (Orchestrator web check, tempers batch A's 'clear 5'.)
ideas.resources: laptop only, free.

ideas.title: p-bit network as a physical Gibbs sampler: exact test
ideas.question: Does a small simulated p-bit network reproduce exact Gibbs probabilities?
ideas.hook: Implement a small software p-bit network (asynchronous stochastic-sigmoid units, as proposed for probabilistic-bit hardware) for a toy Ising system, and compare its empirical stationary distribution against the exact Boltzmann…
ideas.firstMonth: Week1: implement asynchronous p-bit/Gibbs updates for a small Ising ring (4-8 spins). Week2: enumerate the exact Boltzmann distribution and compare via KL divergence to the p-bit histogram. Week3: sweep the p-bit gain/temperature parameter and study convergence rate. Week4: wire the same update rule into training a tiny RBM on a toy binary dataset.
ideas.experiment: Implement a small software p-bit network (asynchronous stochastic-sigmoid units, as proposed for probabilistic-bit hardware) for a toy Ising system, and compare its empirical stationary distribution against the exact Boltzmann distribution from brute-force enumeration. The question: does the same asynchronous update rule, pushed into training a tiny Restricted Boltzmann Machine, sample as well as textbook Gibbs sampling?
ideas.baseline: Brute-force enumeration gives the exact target distribution for small systems, making sampler accuracy fully checkable.
ideas.publicationPath: Characterize how p-bit sampling accuracy/speed scales with network size and connectivity vs standard Gibbs sampling, and whether it gives a wall-clock or sample-efficiency edge for RBM training; workshop/PRE-class paper connecting to neuromorphic ML.
ideas.risk: The RBM-training extension may be a weak result if the toy dataset is too small to show a clear speed/quality edge; mitigated by keeping the exact-distribution comparison as the guaranteed rung-1 deliverable.
ideas.pivot: Use the first month to test whether the proposed comparison is feasible and distinct from earlier work; discuss scope changes with a mentor.
ideas.resources: laptop only, free (software p-bit simulation, not a physical build — that variant belongs to D06).

ideas.title: Do noisy coupled oscillators sample a Boltzmann distribution?
ideas.question: Do noisy coupled oscillators produce a Boltzmann distribution?
ideas.hook: Simulate a network of noisy coupled phase oscillators (Kuramoto-style, each phase bin mapped to an Ising spin) and test whether its long-time phase histogram matches the Boltzmann distribution of the corresponding Ising Hamiltonian at an…
ideas.firstMonth: First validate a tiny oscillator model and its phase-to-spin mapping with a mentor. Enumerate the corresponding proposed binary target, compare empirical joint probabilities with independent runs, and only then sweep noise or coupling strength.
ideas.experiment: Simulate a network of noisy coupled phase oscillators (Kuramoto-style, each phase bin mapped to an Ising spin) and test whether its long-time phase histogram matches the Boltzmann distribution of the corresponding Ising Hamiltonian at an effective temperature set by the noise strength. Compare sampling quality (KL divergence, mixing time) against a standard Metropolis Gibbs sampler on the same small instances.
ideas.baseline: Exact enumeration provides a binary target distribution once the Hamiltonian and oscillator-to-spin mapping are specified. Compare with an explicit Metropolis sampler and independent-run mixing diagnostics; matching a target is an empirical test, not guaranteed by phase binning.
ideas.publicationPath: Extend to larger/structured instances and quantify 'Boltzmann-likeness' vs network size and noise color (white vs 1/f), connecting to the noise-enhanced physical Ising-machine literature; PRE-class paper or workshop note.

Validate the dynamics, phase-to-spin mapping, and target distribution first; then separate poor mixing from distribution mismatch. Synchronization may collapse sampling, and a null result alone does not guarantee publication.
ideas.pivot: Push past KL-divergence-vs-noise curves to explicitly mapping the synchronization-onset boundary where Boltzmann-likeness breaks down, tying the null result to the noise-enhanced-Ising-machine literature's own open sampling-quality question.

ideas.title: Digital memcomputing solves 3-SAT: chaos and speed
ideas.question: How are chaos and solution speed related in a digital memcomputing solver?
ideas.hook: Implement a digital memcomputing machine (DMM) — coupled nonlinear ODEs with memory whose point attractors are satisfying assignments — for random 3-SAT, and benchmark its time-to-solution scaling near the satisfiability threshold against…
ideas.firstMonth: Week1-2: implement SA and WalkSAT on random 3-SAT, establishing the baseline and the easy-hard-easy curve near threshold (tutorial-sized). Week3: implement the DMM ODE system for small 3-SAT instances from the published equations. Week4: verify the DMM reproduces a published TTS or scaling result on a handful of small instances.
ideas.experiment: Implement a digital memcomputing machine (DMM) — coupled nonlinear ODEs with memory whose point attractors are satisfying assignments — for random 3-SAT, and benchmark its time-to-solution scaling near the satisfiability threshold against WalkSAT and simulated annealing, while measuring the largest Lyapunov exponent of the chaotic transient DMM exhibits before locking onto a solution.
ideas.baseline: 3-SAT satisfiability is exactly checkable (assignments verify in linear time; threshold ratio is well characterized); TTS and Lyapunov exponents are objective computed quantities.
ideas.publicationPath: Systematic TTS-scaling comparison (DMM vs WalkSAT vs SA) across sizes at the SAT/UNSAT threshold plus Lyapunov-exponent characterization of the DMM transient — extends the PI's own DMM numerical-stability work; plausible Chaos/PRE-class paper with sustained junior-level effort and close mentoring.
ideas.risk: DMM ODE integration is genuinely stiff and its stability is itself an open research topic per the cited PI paper — ambitious for an undergrad; mitigated by keeping SA/WalkSAT as the guaranteed fail-soft rungs 1-2 and requiring heavy mentoring (hence junior+ only).
ideas.pivot: Use the first month to test whether the proposed comparison is feasible and distinct from earlier work; discuss scope changes with a mentor.
ideas.resources: laptop/GPU for larger instances, free (ODE integration only).

ideas.title: One knob, two goals: SA schedules for sampling vs optimizing
ideas.question: Can one annealing schedule serve both optimization and sampling?
ideas.hook: Run the same simulated-annealing code on small Ising/Max-Cut instances under several schedules (fast-linear, slow-linear, exponential, adaptive) and measure two different things from the same runs: ground-state-finding success probability…
ideas.firstMonth: Week1: fast-linear SA schedule on small Ising instances, ground state via brute force. Week2: add exponential/logarithmic schedules. Week3: measure success-probability curves per schedule. Week4: for a small enough instance, compute the exact Boltzmann distribution and measure the multi-restart SA ensemble's KL divergence from it, per schedule.
ideas.experiment: Run the same simulated-annealing code on small Ising/Max-Cut instances under several schedules (fast-linear, slow-linear, exponential, adaptive) and measure two different things from the same runs: ground-state-finding success probability ('optimizing') and how closely the multi-restart final-state ensemble matches the true low-T Boltzmann distribution ('sampling'). The question: is any schedule good at both at once?
ideas.baseline: Brute-force ground state and exact Boltzmann distribution for small N give fully objective, machine-checkable scores for both goals.
ideas.publicationPath: Extend to spin-glass instances and classic adaptive-schedule families, mapping the optimize/sample Pareto frontier for SA; workshop or JSTAT-style methods note.
ideas.risk: Exact Boltzmann comparison is only feasible for small N, so the sampling rung stays a controlled proof-of-concept rather than a large-scale claim — acceptable for a first result.
ideas.pivot: Use the first month to test whether the proposed comparison is feasible and distinct from earlier work; discuss scope changes with a mentor.
ideas.resources: laptop only, free.

ideas.title: How hard is a planted spin glass? A scaling law
ideas.question: What determines the difficulty of spin-glass instances with a known solution?
ideas.hook: Build a small planted-solution spin-glass generator (plant a known ground state, then add frustrated couplings that keep it optimal, following the planted-benchmark literature) and measure how SA's time-to-solution scales with instance…
ideas.firstMonth: Week1: random-bond Ising SA baseline with brute-force verification on tiny instances. Week2: implement a simple planted-solution generator. Week3: sweep the hardness parameter and record SA success probability/TTS. Week4: fit TTS-vs-size scaling and compare planted vs random instances at fixed size.
ideas.experiment: Build a small planted-solution spin-glass generator (plant a known ground state, then add frustrated couplings that keep it optimal, following the planted-benchmark literature) and measure how SA's time-to-solution scales with instance size and a tunable 'hardness' parameter, comparing planted vs unplanted random instances of the same size.
ideas.baseline: The planted ground state is known by construction, so success/failure is exactly checkable without brute force even at larger N.
ideas.publicationPath: Extend to larger planted ensembles and additional solvers (the SB solver from D05-05) to build a public planted-instance TTS benchmark with a fitted hardness law; PRE/Frontiers-style methods paper, directly reusable by the whole cohort.
ideas.risk: A planted instance can be trivially easy if not tuned carefully; mitigated by following the published construction closely and empirically validating hardness in week 3.
ideas.pivot: Planted-instance TTS benchmarking is well-trodden infrastructure; make the fitted hardness-vs-frustration-parameter scaling law itself (exponential vs sub-exponential form, with error bars) the paper's claim rather than the benchmark's existence.
ideas.resources: laptop only, free.

ideas.title: 8-Node Coupled-Oscillator Ising Machine on a Breadboard
ideas.question: Can eight breadboard oscillators solve a small Ising problem?
ideas.hook: Build a small breadboard array of resistively coupled relaxation oscillators (555-timer or Schmitt-trigger RC circuits) whose locked phases encode spins, and read out the network's steady state as a candidate Max-Cut solution for a…
ideas.firstMonth: Breadboard 4 RC relaxation oscillators, wire a resistor-network coupling matrix for a 4-node graph, capture phase via a microphone or Arduino ADC, and check that locking states match a brute-force Max-Cut answer.
ideas.experiment: Build a small breadboard array of resistively coupled relaxation oscillators (555-timer or Schmitt-trigger RC circuits) whose locked phases encode spins, and read out the network's steady state as a candidate Max-Cut solution for a hand-picked graph. The open question is whether deliberately added electronic noise helps the analog network escape local minima the way thermal noise helps a real annealer, and how that trades off against solution quality as the graph scales from 4 to 16 nodes.
ideas.baseline: Exact brute-force or ILP Max-Cut solutions for graphs up to ~16 nodes give a machine-checkable optimum to compare the oscillator network's output against.
ideas.publicationPath: Scale to 8-16 oscillators, benchmark time-to-solution vs. graph density against a software simulated-annealing/Ising baseline (pairs with a D05-style team), and characterize how injected noise amplitude changes ground-state hit rate; target a workshop paper (e.g. an unconventional/neuromorphic computing venue) or a short Chaos communication.

ideas.title: Rolling-Platform Metronome Array Tests the Kuramoto Model
ideas.question: How closely do real metronomes follow a synchronization model?
ideas.hook: Track eight metronomes on a board that rolls freely on cans with an overhead webcam, and measure the Kuramoto order parameter as a function of coupling strength (board mass/friction) and frequency spread.
ideas.firstMonth: Assemble 4-8 wind-up metronomes on a rolling platform (board on soda cans), record video, extract each pendulum's phase via peak detection in OpenCV, and plot the order parameter r(t) for a first coupling setting.
ideas.experiment: Track eight metronomes on a board that rolls freely on cans with an overhead webcam, and measure the Kuramoto order parameter as a function of coupling strength (board mass/friction) and frequency spread. The question is whether splitting the metronomes into two weakly linked subgroups produces a stable chimera-like partial-synchronization state, as seen numerically for 100 coupled metronomes but rarely tested experimentally at small numbers.
ideas.baseline: The Kuramoto model gives an exact analytic critical-coupling formula in the mean-field limit, so deviations of the measured transition are directly quantifiable.
ideas.publicationPath: Scan coupling strength and frequency detuning to trace the full synchronization transition, fit it to the mean-field Kuramoto prediction, then split the array into two subgroups searching for chimera-like states; target American Journal of Physics or Chaos, the established venue for this exact system.
ideas.risk: Only 4-8 metronomes are affordable, limiting statistics on the transition; cheap units have nonuniform friction/rate that must be characterized first.
ideas.pivot: Use the first month to test whether the proposed comparison is feasible and distinct from earlier work; discuss scope changes with a mentor.
ideas.resources: 8 wind-up metronomes (~¥30 each) or DIY servo pendulums, board + cans, webcam; roughly ¥400-700.

ideas.title: Chladni-Plate Physical Reservoir for Digit Classification
ideas.question: Can vibrations in a plate provide useful features for classification?
ideas.hook: Drive a thin plate with a coil exciter, photograph the sand nodal (Chladni) pattern at each frequency, and use the resulting pattern as a fixed random feature map that a linear classifier reads out to distinguish a small set of…
ideas.firstMonth: Build the plate + exciter + sand rig, sweep frequency, photograph nodal patterns, and cross-check the measured resonant frequencies against thin-plate (Kirchhoff-Love) theory as a calibration step.
ideas.experiment: Drive a thin plate with a coil exciter, photograph the sand nodal (Chladni) pattern at each frequency, and use the resulting pattern as a fixed random feature map that a linear classifier reads out to distinguish a small set of frequency-encoded input signals. The question is whether classification accuracy peaks near a particular mode density, linking a device usually used to demonstrate eigenmodes to a genuine, if small, physical-reservoir computation.
ideas.baseline: Measured nodal-line patterns and resonant frequencies are checked against exact plate-vibration eigenmode predictions, giving an objective calibration and sanity check for every run.
ideas.publicationPath: Encode a small input set (e.g. stroke-pressure-modulated frequency sweeps) and train a linear/logistic readout on the resulting Chladni-pattern features for a 3-5 class task, benchmarking accuracy against a digital random-feature baseline of matched size; target a physical/unconventional-computing workshop or the Journal of the Acoustical Society, following the rigorous-characterization precedent in the cited work.
ideas.risk: Hysteresis in sand-pattern formation across repeated frequency sweeps may hurt feature reproducibility; the classification task must stay small to remain tractable in weeks.
ideas.pivot: Use the first month to test whether the proposed comparison is feasible and distinct from earlier work; discuss scope changes with a mentor.
ideas.resources: Thin metal/acrylic plate, small speaker exciter + amp, fine sand or semolina, function generator (or Arduino DDS), webcam; roughly ¥500-900.

ideas.title: Bristlebot Swarm as a Collision-Based Random-Walk Computer
ideas.question: Can a group of bristlebots implement a useful random-walk computation?
ideas.hook: Build a swarm of 15-20 vibration-motor bristlebots in a bounded arena and use an overhead webcam to track collisions between labeled sub-groups, aiming to realize a simple majority-vote logic gate from the collision statistics.
ideas.firstMonth: Build 4-6 bristlebots (toothbrush head + pager motor + coin cell), overhead-track trajectories in a small arena, and measure mean free path and collision rate versus density.
ideas.experiment: Build a swarm of 15-20 vibration-motor bristlebots in a bounded arena and use an overhead webcam to track collisions between labeled sub-groups, aiming to realize a simple majority-vote logic gate from the collision statistics. The question is how swarm density and arena geometry set the reliability of this collision-based computation, connecting hobbyist active-matter robots to the classic billiard-ball-computer idea.
ideas.baseline: Collision statistics are compared against a matched-density hard-disk / active-Brownian-particle simulation, and the logic-gate output is checked against the exact expected majority-function truth table.
ideas.publicationPath: Scale to 15-20 bots, design and demonstrate a minimal majority-vote gate realized by labeled-group collision events, and characterize its reliability versus density/arena shape against the active-matter literature; target a workshop paper (Artificial Life / unconventional computing) or a short PRE communication.
ideas.risk: Motor-to-motor variability creates uncontrolled heterogeneity; demonstrating a reliable logic gate may need many repeated trials for adequate statistics.
ideas.pivot: Use the first month to test whether the proposed comparison is feasible and distinct from earlier work; discuss scope changes with a mentor.
ideas.resources: 15-20 pager motors + toothbrush heads + coin cells + tape, cardboard arena, webcam; roughly ¥400-800.

ideas.title: Single-Node Delay-Line Optoelectronic Reservoir Computer
ideas.question: Can a single optoelectronic delay loop serve as a reservoir computer?
ideas.hook: Build a single nonlinear optoelectronic node (LED/photodiode plus op-amp) wrapped in a long electronic time-delay feedback loop, time-multiplex it into 50-100 virtual nodes, and benchmark the resulting delay-based reservoir computer on…
ideas.firstMonth: Build and characterize the single nonlinear node's transfer function (LED-photodiode or transistor saturation curve), assemble a delay line (analog delay chip or microcontroller-emulated shift register), and verify the time-multiplexed masking scheme reproduces a known simple nonlinear map.
ideas.experiment: Build a single nonlinear optoelectronic node (LED/photodiode plus op-amp) wrapped in a long electronic time-delay feedback loop, time-multiplex it into 50-100 virtual nodes, and benchmark the resulting delay-based reservoir computer on standard NARMA10/Mackey-Glass prediction tasks. The question is how much of the published photonic-reservoir performance a sub-¥1500 electronic breadboard version can recover, and where component noise caps the achievable memory capacity.
ideas.baseline: NARMA10 and Mackey-Glass are standard published benchmarks with well-defined NMSE/NRMSE metrics, allowing direct, literature-comparable scoring of the hardware.
ideas.publicationPath: Run the full delay-based reservoir-computing pipeline on NARMA10/Mackey-Glass benchmarks, systematically vary delay length, virtual-node count, and feedback gain versus prediction NMSE, and compare against the cited optoelectronic results and a digital echo-state-network baseline; target Neuromorphic Computing and Engineering or Chaos.
ideas.risk: Electronic noise floor and limited virtual-node count may cap benchmark performance well below published results; this is the most electronics-heavy build in the set, hence flagged as the ambitious junior project.
ideas.pivot: Use the first month to test whether the proposed comparison is feasible and distinct from earlier work; discuss scope changes with a mentor.

ideas.title: Marble-Run Mechanical Adder as a Landauer-Bound Testbed
ideas.question: What can a mechanical marble-run adder reveal about energy use?
ideas.hook: Build a 2-3 bit gravity-driven marble-run binary adder from cardboard/3D-printed parts, and measure the energy input (drop height, friction) and error rate per logic operation over many trials.
ideas.firstMonth: Build one mechanical NOT/AND gate from cardboard, LEGO, or 3D-printed parts and marbles, measure its input-output truth table over 50+ trials, and estimate energy input from drop height and marble mass.
ideas.experiment: Build a 2-3 bit gravity-driven marble-run binary adder from cardboard/3D-printed parts, and measure the energy input (drop height, friction) and error rate per logic operation over many trials. The question is how many orders of magnitude above the Landauer bound (kT ln 2) a purely mechanical room-temperature gate sits, and whether slowing the marbles trades speed for measurably lower dissipation as thermodynamics predicts.
ideas.baseline: Landauer's bound (kT ln 2 per erased bit) is an exact theoretical floor, and each gate's truth table gives an exact correctness ground truth per trial.
ideas.publicationPath: Assemble a full 2-3 bit adder, sweep marble speed/track friction to trace an experimental dissipation-vs-error-rate curve, and compare the extrapolated per-operation energy floor to kT ln 2 and to published micro-electromechanical logic-gate numbers; target American Journal of Physics as a pedagogical thermodynamics-of-computation demonstration.
ideas.risk: The macroscopic energy scale sits astronomically above kT ln 2, so results are an order-of-magnitude scaling demonstration rather than a precision fundamental-limit test; claims must stay modest.
ideas.pivot: Use the first month to test whether the proposed comparison is feasible and distinct from earlier work; discuss scope changes with a mentor.
ideas.resources: Cardboard/foam board or basic 3D printing, glass marbles, DIY IR photogate for timing; roughly ¥200-400.

ideas.title: LED-Lattice Hardware Realization of Rule 110 Under Noise
ideas.question: How robust is a physical Rule 110 cellular automaton to noise?
ideas.hook: Implement the proven Turing-complete elementary cellular automaton Rule 110 on a real clocked LED-strip lattice (Arduino/FPGA-driven), reproduce a known glider collision exactly, then inject controlled per-step bit-flip noise.
ideas.firstMonth: Wire an 8-16 pixel WS2812 LED strip to an Arduino, implement the Rule 110 update logic, and reproduce a known glider collision on the physical strip, matching it exactly against the textbook noiseless trajectory.
ideas.experiment: Implement the proven Turing-complete elementary cellular automaton Rule 110 on a real clocked LED-strip lattice (Arduino/FPGA-driven), reproduce a known glider collision exactly, then inject controlled per-step bit-flip noise. The question is what noise level destroys Rule 110's glider-based computations, and whether a simple local-majority repair rule measurably raises that fault-tolerance threshold.
ideas.baseline: Rule 110's update table is exact and its Turing-universality is a proven theorem, so any deviation of the hardware trajectory from the ideal noiseless one is unambiguously measurable.
ideas.publicationPath: Scale to 64-128 pixels, sweep injected bit-flip probability per step, measure glider survival/computation fidelity versus noise, and test a local-majority-vote repair scheme against the noise threshold; target a workshop paper at an automata/unconventional-computing venue, framed as an experimental fault-tolerance study of a proven-universal CA.
ideas.risk: WS2812 update latency or timing jitter could itself act as an uncontrolled noise source, confounding the deliberately injected noise; the hardware noise floor must be characterized first.
ideas.pivot: Use the first month to test whether the proposed comparison is feasible and distinct from earlier work; discuss scope changes with a mentor.
ideas.resources: WS2812 LED strip (1-2 m), Arduino/ESP32, breadboard/wires; roughly ¥150-300.

ideas.title: Noisy-Comparator p-Bit Array for Boltzmann Sampling
ideas.question: Can noisy comparator circuits sample a small Boltzmann distribution?
ideas.hook: Build an array of 8-16 free-running noisy comparators ("p-bits"), using amplified transistor/diode noise as the stochastic element, resistively coupled to encode a small hand-picked Ising Hamiltonian, and sample the network over time to…
ideas.firstMonth: Build one p-bit (amplified noise into a comparator with a bias input) and characterize its output probability as a function of bias, confirming it follows the expected sigmoidal p-bit response curve.
ideas.experiment: Build an array of 8-16 free-running noisy comparators ("p-bits"), using amplified transistor/diode noise as the stochastic element, resistively coupled to encode a small hand-picked Ising Hamiltonian, and sample the network over time to reconstruct its Boltzmann distribution. The question is whether the hardware's sampled distribution and ground-state hit rate on a small planted instance match exact Boltzmann statistics closely enough to be useful, and how that fidelity degrades as more p-bits are added.
ideas.baseline: For small (≤16-spin) Hamiltonians, the exact Boltzmann distribution and ground state are computable by brute force, giving a direct fidelity metric for the hardware sampler.
ideas.publicationPath: Couple 8-16 p-bits with a resistor-network weight matrix encoding a small planted Ising instance, sample and compare the empirical distribution/ground-state hit rate to exact Boltzmann statistics and a software Gibbs-sampler baseline, and characterize sampling speed versus effective temperature/coupling; target a workshop paper on probabilistic/unconventional computing, ideally alongside a software-Ising-benchmark team.
ideas.risk: Comparator/transistor noise may not be tunable enough to sweep an effective temperature, and cross-talk between closely spaced analog p-bits could bias the sampled distribution.
ideas.pivot: Use the first month to test whether the proposed comparison is feasible and distinct from earlier work; discuss scope changes with a mentor.
ideas.resources: Transistors/diodes for noise sources, comparator ICs, resistor-DAC coupling network, Arduino/DAQ for logging; roughly ¥400-700.

ideas.title: Computational-capability map of Life-like CA rules
ideas.question: Which Life-like cellular automata support useful computation?
ideas.hook: Sweep the outer-totalistic 2-state Life-like rule family, simulate each from random and structured seeds, and score three cheap complexity proxies (mean-field Langton's lambda, entropy growth rate, zlib compression ratio of the space-time…
ideas.firstMonth: Write a fast numpy/bitwise 2D life-like CA simulator; reproduce Conway's Life (B3/S23), a chaotic rule, and a frozen rule as three sanity-check classes; compute compression-ratio and entropy-growth curves for each and confirm they land in the expected order.
ideas.experiment: Sweep the outer-totalistic 2-state Life-like rule family, simulate each from random and structured seeds, and score three cheap complexity proxies (mean-field Langton's lambda, entropy growth rate, zlib compression ratio of the space-time diagram) to sort every rule into Wolfram's four classes without human labeling. The question: do purely statistical proxies recover the known class of canonical rules (Life is class IV, rule-30-like chaos, frozen rules), and where do the proxies disagree with each other?
ideas.baseline: Compression ratio, entropy growth rate, and downstream task accuracy are deterministic functions of the simulated trajectory, checkable against textbook Wolfram-class labels for ~15 canonical rules.
ideas.publicationPath: A systematic complexity-proxy sweep across the outer-totalistic rule space, cross-validated against literature-labeled classes and a downstream computational-capability benchmark (density-classification or synchronization score per rule); target venue: ALIFE conference / Artificial Life journal short paper.
ideas.risk: complexity proxies can disagree sharply near the class-III/IV boundary; mitigate by reporting disagreement itself as a finding rather than forcing a single label.
ideas.pivot: Compression/entropy-vs-Wolfram-class sweeps of Life-like rule space already exist (Wuensche, Zenil); make the downstream computational-capability cross-validation (density-classification/sync score correlated with the proxies) the headline, not the proxy sweep.
ideas.resources: laptop only, no GPU or API needed, ~0 cost

ideas.title: Regeneration scaling law for growing neural CA
ideas.question: How does the repair ability of a neural cellular automaton scale?
ideas.hook: Train a small convolutional update-rule neural cellular automaton to grow a target 2D image from a single seed cell and to regrow after damage, then systematically wound trained models at varying sizes/locations and varying training-time…
ideas.firstMonth: Follow a tutorial-sized differentiable-CA training script (PyTorch, small images e.g. 28x28) to train a single grow-from-seed NCA model and confirm it reaches a stable target pattern.
ideas.experiment: Train a small convolutional update-rule neural cellular automaton to grow a target 2D image from a single seed cell and to regrow after damage, then systematically wound trained models at varying sizes/locations and varying training-time damage-augmentation rates to measure a quantitative regeneration-success curve. The question: is there a sharp threshold in training-time damage exposure below which regeneration collapses, i.e. a phase-transition-like scaling law for robustness?
ideas.baseline: Regeneration success is an exact pixel-distance-to-target threshold, machine-scored after a fixed number of post-damage steps.
ideas.publicationPath: A systematic regeneration-robustness scaling study across damage-augmentation rate, wound size, and model capacity, framed as a repair/no-repair phase diagram; target venue: ALIFE conference / workshop, possibly extended to a short journal note.
ideas.risk: NCA training can diverge into chaotic states; mitigate with established stability tricks (state clipping, stochastic cell updates) from the literature.
ideas.pivot: Original Growing NCA already trains with damage augmentation and shows regeneration qualitatively, so the only unclaimed piece is a quantitative sharp-threshold curve in damage-rate x wound-size x capacity space; make the phase-boundary fit (not the regeneration demo itself) the deliverable.

ideas.title: Building and extending logic gates from Life gliders
ideas.question: Can Life gliders form reliable, extensible logic gates?
ideas.hook: Implement classical glider-collision AND/OR/NOT constructions in Conway's Game of Life, verify each by brute-force simulating every input combination against its truth table, then chain gates into a minimal 1-bit adder and benchmark its…
ideas.firstMonth: Build a fast Life simulator with an RLE pattern-file loader, reproduce a published AND-gate glider collision from a public pattern library, and verify its truth table by direct simulation over all 4 input combinations.
ideas.experiment: Implement classical glider-collision AND/OR/NOT constructions in Conway's Game of Life, verify each by brute-force simulating every input combination against its truth table, then chain gates into a minimal 1-bit adder and benchmark its clock period and footprint; as the ambitious extension, search for an equivalent gate construction in a second Life-like rule (e.g. HighLife) where none is published. The question: how much smaller/faster can a verified adder be than the textbook construction, and does collision logic even transfer to a neighboring rule?
ideas.baseline: Fully exact: every constructed gate is checked against its truth table by direct simulation, no ambiguity.
ideas.publicationPath: A verified, benchmarked circuit-construction toolkit (simulate-any-Life-like-rule plus automatic truth-table verifier) plus either a faster known-rule adder or a first gate construction in a second rule; target venue: Artificial Life journal / Complex Systems.
ideas.risk: searching a new rule for equivalent collisions is open-ended and may not yield a publishable result in time; the reproduce-then-benchmark-then-search ladder guarantees a result even if the extension fails.
ideas.pivot: Use the first month to test whether the proposed comparison is feasible and distinct from earlier work; discuss scope changes with a mentor.
ideas.resources: laptop only, ~0 cost, heaviest mentoring load of the ten ideas

ideas.title: Phase diagram of particle-life clustering
ideas.question: Where do different collective patterns appear in a particle-life model?
ideas.hook: Implement a minimal particle-life simulator (point particles, a few species, a pairwise attraction/repulsion force table) and sweep the interaction-matrix parameters to map a phase diagram (gas / static clusters / traveling blobs /…
ideas.firstMonth: Implement a vectorized 2D particle-life simulator (numpy, a few hundred particles, 2-3 species) reproducing the qualitative clustering/chasing behaviors from public particle-life demos, and compute a first cluster-size histogram.
ideas.experiment: Implement a minimal particle-life simulator (point particles, a few species, a pairwise attraction/repulsion force table) and sweep the interaction-matrix parameters to map a phase diagram (gas / static clusters / traveling blobs / frozen) using a distance-based cluster-size order parameter and the pair-correlation function. The question: does the transition between static clusters and traveling/chasing phases show finite-size scaling analogous to real motility-induced phase separation in active matter, in a toy rule with no physics built in?
ideas.baseline: Cluster-size distribution and pair-correlation function are exact deterministic functions of the simulated trajectory; finite-size scaling gives a numerically checkable exponent.
ideas.publicationPath: A quantitative phase diagram with finite-size-scaling exponents for the particle-life toy model, compared against known motility-induced phase separation universality classes; target venue: Physical Review E / Artificial Life journal.
ideas.risk: particle-life dynamics can be numerically stiff or blow up for some interaction matrices; needs a stable integrator and force clipping.
ideas.pivot: Narrow to extracting and reporting fitted finite-size-scaling exponents at the static-cluster/traveling-blob transition against a specific named MIPS universality class, rather than a broad four-phase map, so the numeric exponent match/mismatch is the headline result.

ideas.question: How does computation change near the edge of chaos in Boolean networks?
ideas.hook: Build Kauffman NK random Boolean networks, sweep mean connectivity K and bias p, compute the Derrida sensitivity coefficient to locate the exact order/chaos boundary, then measure a downstream computation-capacity proxy (short-term memory…

The question: does computational capacity peak sharply at the predicted critical K=2 line, or is the peak shifted/broadened once measured directly?

ideas.title: Elementary-CA reservoir-computing benchmark sweep
ideas.question: Which elementary cellular automata make useful reservoir computers?
ideas.hook: Wire up all 256 elementary 1D CA rules as reservoirs using the established ECA-reservoir encoding (random input projection into automaton initial conditions, linear readout), benchmark each on memory-capacity and a NARMA-style nonlinear…

ideas.experiment: Wire up all 256 elementary 1D CA rules as reservoirs using the established ECA-reservoir encoding (random input projection into automaton initial conditions, linear readout), benchmark each on memory-capacity and a NARMA-style nonlinear task, and correlate performance against each rule's Wolfram class / Langton-lambda value. The question: do the best reservoir rules cluster at class-IV complex rules as predicted, or does the best measured computation come from unexpectedly simple or chaotic rules?
ideas.baseline: Memory capacity and NARMA prediction error are exact numerical scores from simulated reservoir states and a linear-regression readout, no subjective judgment.
ideas.publicationPath: A full 256-rule sweep correlating reservoir performance with CA classification metrics, released as an open benchmark table; target venue: workshop paper at a reservoir-computing/ALIFE venue, or a short PRE/Chaos paper.
ideas.risk: linear-regression readouts can overfit short benchmark sequences; needs held-out test sequences and multiple independent trials per rule for a stable score.
ideas.pivot: Use the first month to test whether the proposed comparison is feasible and distinct from earlier work; discuss scope changes with a mentor.

ideas.hook: Evolve populations of multi-species Lenia creatures under two conditions, novelty-selection (quality-diversity-style) versus neutral mutation-only drift, and track a compression-based complexity metric of the population's genotypes and…

ideas.title: LLM-proposed rules for the CA density-classification task
ideas.question: Can an AI propose useful cellular-automaton rules for density classification?
ideas.hook: Reimplement the classic 1D binary-state density-classification task (a CA must decide, using only local information, whether the initial configuration has more 1s or 0s), using the published hand-designed and genetic-algorithm-evolved…
ideas.firstMonth: Implement the density-classification task simulator and fitness evaluator (accuracy over random initial configurations of a fixed CA width), and reproduce the published accuracy of the GKL benchmark rule as ground truth.
ideas.experiment: Reimplement the classic 1D binary-state density-classification task (a CA must decide, using only local information, whether the initial configuration has more 1s or 0s), using the published hand-designed and genetic-algorithm-evolved benchmark rules as ground truth, then run an LLM-in-the-loop search where a cheap LLM proposes candidate rule tables and an exact fitness evaluator scores them. The question: can LLM-guided search match or beat the classic evolved rule's ~82-86% accuracy with far fewer evaluations, and are the LLM's rules more interpretable than GA-evolved ones?
ideas.baseline: Classification accuracy on the density task is an exact, fully deterministic metric against a known, published optimum.
ideas.publicationPath: A search-efficiency and interpretability comparison of LLM-guided vs. genetic-algorithm rule search on the density-classification benchmark, including analysis of the strategies the LLM articulates; target venue: ALIFE conference / GECCO workshop.
ideas.risk: LLM-proposed rules may just rediscover the known GKL/GA rules with limited novelty; mitigate by also testing a harder variant (larger neighborhood, non-binary states) with no established benchmark rule.
ideas.pivot: Match-or-beat accuracy against the GKL rule is an easy bar to hit by regurgitation; make the interpretability comparison of LLM-articulated strategies vs. known GA-evolved strategies the paper's core scored contribution.
ideas.resources: laptop plus cheap LLM API calls (~¥50-100/month)

ideas.title: Grokking as a phase transition: order parameter and critical point
ideas.originalDirection: Physics of learning in tiny models
ideas.question: Can a simple measurable quantity reveal the onset of grokking?
ideas.hook: Train a 2-layer MLP or 1-layer transformer on modular addition (mod p) and track test accuracy as a function of training-data fraction and epoch, treating test accuracy as an order parameter.
ideas.firstMonth: Week 1: implement the modular-addition dataset and tiny MLP in PyTorch, reproduce a single grokking run (loss/accuracy curves) on one GPU. Weeks 2-4: sweep training-data fraction, plot generalization epoch vs. fraction, and fit a power law near the critical fraction for a first order-parameter plot.
ideas.experiment: Train a 2-layer MLP or 1-layer transformer on modular addition (mod p) and track test accuracy as a function of training-data fraction and epoch, treating test accuracy as an order parameter. The surprising question: does the sharp memorize-to-generalize jump behave like a genuine second-order phase transition (power-law scaling near a critical data fraction), or is 'sudden' generalization actually a smooth crossover in disguise?
ideas.baseline: Modular arithmetic has an exact answer table; train/test accuracy is computed against ground-truth (a+b) mod p with zero ambiguity.
ideas.publicationPath: Extend to careful critical-exponent estimation (log-log fits with error bars) across several moduli p and task variants; 6-12 month target: a short paper reframing grokking's generalization threshold in critical-phenomena language for a workshop (e.g. ICML/NeurIPS interpretability) or PRE-style venue.
ideas.risk: Grokking timing is sensitive to seed/hyperparameters, so a clean critical-exponent fit may need many repeated runs to average out noise.
ideas.pivot: Use the first month to test whether the proposed comparison is feasible and distinct from earlier work; discuss scope changes with a mentor.
ideas.resources: One consumer GPU (<=24GB) or CPU for the tiny net; free Colab acceptable; no LLM API needed; ~¥0-200 optional cloud credit.

ideas.title: What a tiny transformer linearly encodes from Ising spin configurations
ideas.originalDirection: Physics of learning in tiny models
ideas.question: What information about Ising configurations does a tiny transformer encode?
ideas.hook: Train a small transformer to classify Monte-Carlo-generated 2D Ising spin configurations across temperatures, then fit linear probes to its residual stream to test whether magnetization, energy, and distance-to-Tc are linearly decodable.
ideas.firstMonth: Week 1: generate labeled Ising configurations at various T with a Metropolis sampler; build a tiny transformer classifier. Weeks 2-4: train the classifier, extract residual-stream activations, fit linear probes for magnetization/energy, and plot probe accuracy vs. T.
ideas.experiment: Train a small transformer to classify Monte-Carlo-generated 2D Ising spin configurations across temperatures, then fit linear probes to its residual stream to test whether magnetization, energy, and distance-to-Tc are linearly decodable. The surprising question: does decodability of the order parameter show a sharp transition at the physical critical temperature, mirroring the thermodynamic phase transition inside the network's representations?
ideas.baseline: Onsager's exact solution gives Tc = 2/ln(1+sqrt2) and a closed-form magnetization for the 2D Ising model, so probe predictions can be checked against an exact analytic reference, not just simulation.
ideas.publicationPath: Extend to multiple lattice sizes and models (Ising vs. Potts) to test whether probe-decodability curves finite-size-scale like the physical transition; 6-12 month target: ML4Physics workshop paper or PRE submission on representation-level signatures of physical phase transitions inside trained classifiers.
ideas.risk: A tiny transformer may not need attention at all for this task (a linear model could already classify phases well), making 'what does it represent' less interesting unless probes are designed carefully.
ideas.pivot: Use the first month to test whether the proposed comparison is feasible and distinct from earlier work; discuss scope changes with a mentor.
ideas.resources: One consumer GPU (<=24GB); Metropolis sampler is CPU-cheap; no paid API needed; ~¥0-200.

ideas.title: Finite-size scaling collapse of the grokking transition
ideas.originalDirection: Physics of learning in tiny models
ideas.question: Does the grokking transition follow a finite-size scaling pattern?
ideas.hook: Sweep network width and training-set size for the modular-addition grokking task and look for a finite-size-scaling collapse of the generalization curves onto a single universal curve, the way critical phenomena collapse magnetization…
ideas.firstMonth: Week 1: build a sweep harness that trains many small MLPs at different widths and data fractions on one GPU (short runs each). Weeks 2-4: collect generalization-epoch data across the sweep and attempt a first data-collapse plot, checking collapse quality.
ideas.experiment: Sweep network width and training-set size for the modular-addition grokking task and look for a finite-size-scaling collapse of the generalization curves onto a single universal curve, the way critical phenomena collapse magnetization curves near Tc. ideas.title: Sparse-autoencoder order parameters for an Ising phase classifier
ideas.originalDirection: Physics of learning in tiny models
ideas.question: Can a sparse autoencoder recover an Ising order parameter?
ideas.hook: Train a small CNN to classify 2D Ising configurations as ordered/disordered, then fit a sparse autoencoder to its hidden-layer activations to search for a single monosemantic feature that tracks the true magnetization without ever being…
ideas.firstMonth: Week 1: generate labeled Ising configurations and train the small CNN classifier on one GPU. Weeks 2-4: extract hidden activations, train a small SAE on them, and correlate each learned SAE feature against the true magnetization.
ideas.experiment: Train a small CNN to classify 2D Ising configurations as ordered/disordered, then fit a sparse autoencoder to its hidden-layer activations to search for a single monosemantic feature that tracks the true magnetization without ever being told what magnetization is. The surprising question: does unsupervised sparse-feature discovery recover the known physical order parameter cleanly, or does the network instead encode phase information in a messier, distributed way that SAEs only partially resolve?
ideas.baseline: Magnetization is computed exactly from the spin configuration (mean spin) and Tc is known exactly (Onsager), so the SAE feature can be checked against an unambiguous physical quantity, not visual inspection.
ideas.publicationPath: Extend across lattice sizes and to a second toy system (e.g. XY model) to test generality; 6-12 month target: an ML interpretability workshop paper (or PRE if pushed toward finite-size scaling of the discovered feature) on whether SAE-discovered features recover known physical order parameters.
ideas.risk: With such a simple task the classifier may already be near-linear, so the SAE might trivially find the order parameter; staying novel requires pushing to noisier/harder variants quickly.
ideas.pivot: Use the first month to test whether the proposed comparison is feasible and distinct from earlier work; discuss scope changes with a mentor.

ideas.title: What a small predictor network encodes about chaotic orbits
ideas.originalDirection: Physics of learning in tiny models
ideas.question: What does a small neural predictor learn about chaotic trajectories?
ideas.hook: Train a tiny MLP or transformer to forecast trajectories of a simple chaotic map (logistic or Henon map) or the double pendulum, then probe its hidden units against the numerically exact local Lyapunov exponent and invariant density at…
ideas.firstMonth: Week 1: implement the chaotic map/double-pendulum simulator and compute exact reference Lyapunov exponents via the tangent-map method; train a first tiny predictor on one GPU. Weeks 2-4: probe hidden activations against local divergence rate and produce a first correlation plot.
ideas.experiment: Train a tiny MLP or transformer to forecast trajectories of a simple chaotic map (logistic or Henon map) or the double pendulum, then probe its hidden units against the numerically exact local Lyapunov exponent and invariant density at each point. The surprising question: does accurate short-horizon prediction require the network to implicitly represent local divergence rate (chaos strength), or can it forecast well while staying 'blind' to the underlying chaotic structure?
ideas.baseline: Lyapunov exponents and invariant densities for logistic/Henon maps and the double pendulum are numerically exact/well-converged reference quantities computable independently of the learned model.
ideas.publicationPath: Extend to multiple chaotic systems and prediction horizons, comparing probe strength across the regular-to-chaotic transition; 6-12 month target: a workshop or PRE-style paper on what minimal predictive networks internally encode about chaos, beyond existing prediction-accuracy-only forecasting studies.
ideas.risk: Correlating hidden-unit activity with a continuous quantity like local Lyapunov exponent can be noisy for small networks, so probe results may be weak without careful averaging.
ideas.pivot: Use the first month to test whether the proposed comparison is feasible and distinct from earlier work; discuss scope changes with a mentor.
ideas.resources: One consumer GPU (<=24GB) or CPU; simulators are cheap; no API cost; ~¥0.

ideas.title: Scaling laws for tiny transformers on a synthetic physics task
ideas.originalDirection: Physics of learning in tiny models
ideas.question: How do tiny-transformer performance and compute scale on synthetic physics tasks?
ideas.hook: Train a systematic grid of tiny transformers (roughly 1e3-1e6 parameters, several dataset sizes) on a synthetic physics-generation task (e.g. predicting the next microstate in an Ising Monte Carlo trajectory) and fit power-law scaling…
ideas.firstMonth: Week 1: build the synthetic physics data generator and a minimal, parameterizable transformer training harness that logs params/data/compute/loss on one GPU. Weeks 2-4: run a first small grid (~10-15 runs, each under an hour) and produce a first loss-vs-compute log-log plot.
ideas.experiment: Train a systematic grid of tiny transformers (roughly 1e3-1e6 parameters, several dataset sizes) on a synthetic physics-generation task (e.g. predicting the next microstate in an Ising Monte Carlo trajectory) and fit power-law scaling curves for loss vs. parameters/data/compute. The surprising question: do compute-optimal scaling exponents measured on a small, exactly-generated physics domain match language-model exponents, or does a cleaner ground-truth generative process change them?
ideas.baseline: The synthetic physics generator produces data from a known deterministic/stochastic rule, so the true entropy/irreducible loss floor is known exactly, letting the power-law fit be checked against a known asymptote.
ideas.publicationPath: Scale the grid to ~40-60 runs with careful compute accounting and fit both power laws and the compute-optimal frontier; 6-12 month target: an ambitious ML workshop paper comparing measured exponents on physics-generated data against the original Kaplan et al. language-model exponents, with the junior student as lead.
ideas.risk: Toy-scale scaling laws are notoriously noisy with small models and small grids; getting statistically convincing power-law fits may need more runs than a semester allows, so the ladder should include a qualitative-trend-only fallback rung.
ideas.pivot: Use the first month to test whether the proposed comparison is feasible and distinct from earlier work; discuss scope changes with a mentor.
ideas.resources: One consumer GPU (<=24GB); each run <=1 hour, full 40-60 run grid spread over weeks; no paid API needed; ~¥0-500 optional cloud credit for parallel runs.

ideas.title: Mapping the grokking phase diagram in weight-decay/learning-rate space
ideas.originalDirection: Physics of learning in tiny models
ideas.question: How do learning rate and weight decay change the grokking transition?
ideas.hook: Run a dense grid of modular-addition training runs over weight decay and learning rate, classify each run as 'groks', 'never generalizes', or 'generalizes immediately', and plot the resulting 2D phase diagram with its boundary.
ideas.firstMonth: Week 1: build the grid-sweep harness (weight decay x learning rate) with a fixed modular-addition task/architecture on one GPU. Weeks 2-4: run the first coarse grid (~20-30 short runs), classify outcomes, and plot a first phase-diagram heatmap.
ideas.experiment: Run a dense grid of modular-addition training runs over weight decay and learning rate, classify each run as 'groks', 'never generalizes', or 'generalizes immediately', and plot the resulting 2D phase diagram with its boundary. The surprising question: is the grok/non-grok boundary a sharp, reproducible curve (a genuine phase boundary with a well-defined critical line) or a fuzzy, seed-dependent region?
ideas.baseline: Each grid point's classification (groks / doesn't / immediate) is read off the exact modular-arithmetic test accuracy curve, an objective, reproducible criterion, not a judgment call.
ideas.publicationPath: Refine grid resolution near the boundary and add repeated seeds for boundary-location error bars; 6-12 month target: a workshop or PRE-style paper presenting an explicit, quantitative grokking phase diagram with an estimated critical boundary, extending the qualitative weight-decay finding into a full mapped phase space.
ideas.risk: Boundary sharpness may be seed-dependent, requiring several repeated runs per grid point to get a clean phase diagram rather than a noisy scatter.
ideas.pivot: Use the first month to test whether the proposed comparison is feasible and distinct from earlier work; discuss scope changes with a mentor.
ideas.resources: One consumer GPU (<=24GB); each run minutes, full grid a few GPU-hours; no API cost; ~¥0-200.

ideas.title: Does a trained neural quantum state 'know' the Ising critical point?
ideas.originalDirection: Physics of learning in tiny models
ideas.question: Does a neural quantum state encode an Ising critical point?
ideas.hook: Train a small neural-network quantum-state ansatz (RBM or tiny transformer) by variational Monte Carlo to find ground states of the 1D transverse-field Ising model across field strength h, then probe its hidden representation for…
ideas.firstMonth: Week 1: set up exact diagonalization ground truth for a small TFIM chain (N<=16) and a minimal VMC training loop for an RBM ansatz on one GPU. Weeks 2-4: train the ansatz across a field-strength sweep, benchmark ground-state energy against exact diagonalization, and plot energy accuracy vs. h.
ideas.experiment: Train a small neural-network quantum-state ansatz (RBM or tiny transformer) by variational Monte Carlo to find ground states of the 1D transverse-field Ising model across field strength h, then probe its hidden representation for signatures of the exact critical point (h=1) via linear probes, benchmarked against exact diagonalization for small chains. The surprising question: does the ansatz's internal representation show a detectable change right at the exactly-known quantum critical point, the way classical phase classifiers show representation transitions at Tc?
ideas.baseline: The 1D transverse-field Ising model is exactly solvable (Jordan-Wigner / exact diagonalization for small N), giving exact ground-state energies and the exact critical point h=1 to check the trained ansatz and its probes against.
ideas.publicationPath: Add representation probing (correlation-length decoding) across the sweep and multiple chain lengths for finite-size scaling; 6-12 month target: an ambitious junior-led paper for a quantum-ML workshop or PRB/PRE-style venue on interpretability of neural quantum states near a quantum critical point, extending existing entanglement-structure analyses with explicit probing methodology.
ideas.risk: VMC training for NQS ansatzes can be unstable/slow to converge precisely near the critical point where the interesting physics is, so getting well-converged ground states across the full h-sweep may be the real bottleneck.
ideas.pivot: Use the first month to test whether the proposed comparison is feasible and distinct from earlier work; discuss scope changes with a mentor.
ideas.resources: One consumer GPU (<=24GB); VMC training on small chains runs in hours; no paid API needed; ~¥0-300.

ideas.title: Agent locates the 2D Ising model's critical temperature
ideas.question: Can an agent locate the Ising critical temperature efficiently?
ideas.hook: An LLM agent designs and runs a sequence of Metropolis Monte Carlo experiments — choosing lattice sizes, temperatures, and sample counts under a fixed compute budget — to pin down the 2D Ising model's critical temperature.
ideas.firstMonth: Physics student codes a vectorized 2D Metropolis Ising simulator in NumPy and reproduces the known magnetization curve at L=16; AI student wraps it as a callable tool and has an LLM agent request runs, read back energy/magnetization, and output a running Tc estimate with an error bar.
ideas.experiment: An LLM agent designs and runs a sequence of Metropolis Monte Carlo experiments — choosing lattice sizes, temperatures, and sample counts under a fixed compute budget — to pin down the 2D Ising model's critical temperature. The surprising question is whether an agent-designed adaptive sampling schedule reaches a target precision in fewer total spin-flips than a naive uniform temperature grid at the same total compute.
ideas.baseline: Onsager's exact solution gives Tc = 2/ln(1+sqrt(2)) ≈ 2.269 J/kB for the 2D square-lattice Ising model; the agent's estimate is scored against this closed-form value. Also compare the chosen experiment sequence with fixed or random designs under the same budget; a correct recalled answer is insufficient evidence of scientific discovery.
ideas.publicationPath: 6–12 months: benchmark agent-designed adaptive sampling against fixed-grid and hand-tuned finite-size-scaling schedules across L=8..64, quantify compute-to-target-precision, and extend to the q=3,4 Potts model where Tc shifts; target an AI4Science workshop (NeurIPS/ICLR) or Computer Physics Communications.
ideas.risk: Agent may just reinvent a fixed grid; the compute budget must be tight enough that adaptive sampling has a real, measurable advantage to discover. The textbook answer may already be known to the model. Evaluate its logged experiment choices and compute use, not final-answer recall alone.
ideas.pivot: This is explicitly one of several near-identical agent-does-physics ideas in the same cohort, so differentiate by releasing the adaptive-sampling-vs-fixed-grid comparison as a reusable compute-to-precision benchmark harness rather than a single Ising result.
ideas.resources: laptop CPU only (Metropolis MC on L≤64 lattices runs in seconds); ¥30-70/month cheap LLM API calls; no GPU needed

ideas.title: Agent detects a fake critical point in the XY model
ideas.question: Can an agent avoid mistaking finite-size behavior for a critical point?
ideas.hook: An agent applies its Ising-style critical-exponent-fitting pipeline to the 2D XY model, where there is no true power-law transition, and must instead recognize the fit degrading and pivot to detecting the topological BKT transition via…
ideas.firstMonth: Physics student writes a 2D XY Monte Carlo simulator (Metropolis on angles) and computes the helicity modulus (spin stiffness) vs. temperature for L=8..32; AI student builds the agent's naive 'fit power law, extract nu' pipeline and runs it on the output to see it fail.
ideas.experiment: An agent applies its Ising-style critical-exponent-fitting pipeline to the 2D XY model, where there is no true power-law transition, and must instead recognize the fit degrading and pivot to detecting the topological BKT transition via the exact universal helicity-modulus jump. The surprising question is whether a cheap LLM-agent's own residual analysis can catch that it is fitting the wrong kind of physics.
ideas.baseline: Kosterlitz-Thouless theory predicts an exact universal jump in helicity modulus of 2Tc/pi at the transition; the agent's detected jump location/ratio is scored against this closed-form prediction.
ideas.publicationPath: 6–12 months: formalize a self-check protocol (goodness-of-fit thresholds that trigger a model-class switch) and test it on 3+ toy systems with qualitatively different transitions (Ising 2nd order, XY BKT, first-order q=8 Potts); target PRE or an AI4Science workshop paper on agents that detect when their own physics model is wrong.
ideas.risk: BKT finite-size effects converge notoriously slowly; must use modest L and well-known finite-size correction formulas, or the agent gets a noisy non-answer either way.
ideas.pivot: ML-based BKT detection is a mature sub-literature, so don't compete on 'can ML find the BKT transition' -- keep the spine on the self-check protocol (goodness-of-fit-triggered model-class switch) as a general agent-diagnostic method, with BKT as just one of the three test systems.
ideas.resources: laptop CPU only; ¥70/month cheap LLM API calls; no GPU needed

ideas.title: Agent finds the exact p_c=1/2 in 2D bond percolation
ideas.question: How efficiently can an agent locate the bond-percolation threshold?
ideas.hook: An agent runs a union-find bond-percolation simulator across occupation probability p on a square lattice and must locate the percolation threshold from cluster-size statistics under a fixed sample budget.
ideas.firstMonth: Student writes a union-find bond-percolation simulator (grid graph, randomly occupy edges with probability p, track largest cluster) for L=32..128 and plots the percolation probability curve vs. p; agent gets this as a callable tool and must design a p-grid under a total-sample budget to localize the crossing.
ideas.experiment: An agent runs a union-find bond-percolation simulator across occupation probability p on a square lattice and must locate the percolation threshold from cluster-size statistics under a fixed sample budget. The twist is that, unlike almost every other 'find the critical point' toy problem, this one has an exact rational answer (p_c = 1/2) the agent's estimate can be checked against directly.
ideas.baseline: Kesten's theorem gives the exact bond-percolation threshold p_c = 1/2 on the square lattice; site percolation adds a second, numerically-known-to-high-precision benchmark. Also compare the chosen experiment sequence with fixed or random designs under the same budget; a correct recalled answer is insufficient evidence of scientific discovery.
ideas.publicationPath: 6–12 months: extend to site percolation (p_c known only numerically, ≈0.5927) and continuum percolation, compare the agent's adaptive-search query efficiency against classical finite-size-scaling protocols; target a computational-physics/PRE paper or an American Journal of Physics note (the exact result is a strong pedagogical fit).
ideas.risk: Union-find percolation is almost too easy computationally; a real, tight query/sample budget must be enforced so there is a genuine experiment-design problem rather than 'simulate everything.' The textbook answer may already be known to the model. Evaluate its logged experiment choices and compute use, not final-answer recall alone.
ideas.pivot: Use the first month to test whether the proposed comparison is feasible and distinct from earlier work; discuss scope changes with a mentor.

ideas.title: Agent rediscovers Kepler's third law under a sim budget
ideas.question: Can an agent recover Kepler's third law within a simulation budget?
ideas.hook: A physics student's exact 2-body Newtonian orbit simulator is exposed to an agent as a costly 'run_orbit(a, e)' tool, and the agent must choose which orbits to simulate under a fixed call budget before fitting the data to rediscover…
ideas.firstMonth: Physics student implements a symplectic (leapfrog) 2-body integrator and verifies energy/angular-momentum conservation and known circular-orbit periods; AI student exposes 'run_orbit(a, e) -> period, trajectory' as an agent tool and logs how many calls the agent needs to converge on the power-law exponent within 1%.
ideas.experiment: A physics student's exact 2-body Newtonian orbit simulator is exposed to an agent as a costly 'run_orbit(a, e)' tool, and the agent must choose which orbits to simulate under a fixed call budget before fitting the data to rediscover Kepler's third law. The surprising question is how much an intelligently chosen experiment design beats passive/random sampling at the same total number of simulations.
ideas.baseline: Kepler's third law (T^2 = 4*pi^2*a^3/(GM)) is derivable in closed form from Newtonian mechanics for the 2-body problem; the agent's fitted exponent and constant are scored against this exact value. Also compare the chosen experiment sequence with fixed or random designs under the same budget; a correct recalled answer is insufficient evidence of scientific discovery.
ideas.publicationPath: 6–12 months: generalize to a modified 1/r^n force law and test whether the agent notices deviation from n=2, publish an active-experimental-design-for-symbolic-discovery comparison across 3-4 toy systems; target an AI4Science workshop or a physics education research journal for the pedagogical angle.
ideas.risk: With only two free parameters the law is very easy to fit from a handful of points; the budget must be genuinely tight and noise added, or the experiment-design choice stops mattering. The textbook answer may already be known to the model. Evaluate its logged experiment choices and compute use, not final-answer recall alone.
ideas.pivot: Use the first month to test whether the proposed comparison is feasible and distinct from earlier work; discuss scope changes with a mentor.
ideas.resources: laptop CPU only; ¥30/month cheap LLM API calls

ideas.title: Agent rediscovers the pendulum's anharmonic correction
ideas.question: Does an agent notice when the small-angle pendulum approximation breaks down?
ideas.hook: A physics student's exact large-angle pendulum simulator (elliptic-integral period) is probed by an agent under a query budget, which must rediscover both the small-angle period law and its first anharmonic correction term.
ideas.firstMonth: Physics student codes an ODE (RK4) pendulum simulator and a closed-form elliptic-integral period function to cross-check it; AI student wraps 'measure_period(L, g, theta0)' as an agent tool and has the agent fit T(theta0) starting from small angles.
ideas.experiment: A physics student's exact large-angle pendulum simulator (elliptic-integral period) is probed by an agent under a query budget, which must rediscover both the small-angle period law and its first anharmonic correction term. The surprising question is whether the agent detects, on its own, the amplitude at which the small-angle approximation breaks down rather than blindly trusting the linear law past its validity range.
ideas.baseline: The exact large-angle pendulum period is T = 4*sqrt(L/g)*K(sin(theta0/2)) (complete elliptic integral of the first kind); its Taylor expansion gives the exact anharmonic correction coefficient (1 + theta0^2/16 + ...) the agent's fit is scored against. Also compare the chosen experiment sequence with fixed or random designs under the same budget; a correct recalled answer is insufficient evidence of scientific discovery.
ideas.publicationPath: 6–12 months: extend to a driven/damped pendulum near chaos onset and benchmark symbolic-regression-plus-active-sampling pipelines against known perturbative expansions; target an AI4Science workshop or American Journal of Physics (the exact elliptic-integral ground truth is a natural fit).
ideas.risk: The agent might fit a generic polynomial rather than the physically meaningful elliptic-integral series; scoring must check coefficient recovery, not just curve-fit R^2. The textbook answer may already be known to the model. Evaluate its logged experiment choices and compute use, not final-answer recall alone.
ideas.pivot: Law-rediscovery-by-agent is a well-trodden genre (AI Feynman, Schmidt-Lipson); make the self-detected breakdown of the linear approximation (does the agent notice and re-query at larger amplitude) the headline metric rather than coefficient-recovery accuracy alone.
ideas.resources: laptop CPU only; ¥30/month cheap LLM API calls

ideas.title: Matched-compute replication audit of a self-improving-agent claim
ideas.question: Does a self-improving-agent claim survive a matched-compute replication?
ideas.hook: The junior picks one recent, compute-heavy claim that an LLM agent improves itself (e.g. via self-play or self-generated training data), builds a matched-compute (not matched-everything) replication at 1-2% of the original scale, and…
ideas.firstMonth: Read the target paper's method section and pick the smallest sub-claim that is checkable in days (e.g. one self-improvement iteration on a narrow, auto-gradable task); build the matched-compute pipeline skeleton and run the no-self-improvement baseline arm first to fix the eval harness and rule out train/test leakage.
ideas.experiment: The junior picks one recent, compute-heavy claim that an LLM agent improves itself (e.g. via self-play or self-generated training data), builds a matched-compute (not matched-everything) replication at 1-2% of the original scale, and scores the paper against a structured leakage/robustness checklist. The surprising question is whether the headline effect survives at reduced scale under a leakage-audited evaluation, or shrinks toward noise.
ideas.baseline: Ground truth is the checklist-scored presence/absence of leakage plus the measured effect size with confidence intervals from the student's own matched-compute runs, directly comparable (same metric, same benchmark) to the original paper's reported numbers.
ideas.publicationPath: 6–12 months: complete 2-3 replication audits across different papers with the same checklist and publish a replication-report-card methodology paper plus the individual findings; target a reproducibility-focused venue (MLRC-style workshop, ReScience C) or a short comment/erratum if a genuine issue is found.
ideas.risk: The original paper's code/data may not be reproducible at all even at small scale, or the compute budget may be too tight for a fair matched-compute comparison; mitigate by picking a claim with public code and a narrow, cheap sub-claim first.
ideas.pivot: Use the first month to test whether the proposed comparison is feasible and distinct from earlier work; discuss scope changes with a mentor.
ideas.resources: one GPU (rented or lab-shared) for replication runs, roughly ¥1000-2000 compute budget, plus cheap LLM API calls for any agent components; ¥3-5 mentor h/wk given the scope

ideas.title: Numeric self-consistency auditor for physics-ML papers
ideas.question: Can a program find numerical inconsistencies in physics and ML papers?
ideas.hook: An agent scans a curated set of arXiv physics-ML papers, extracts every pair of numbers that should be arithmetically consistent (a reported percentage improvement vs. the raw before/after numbers, or subgroup counts vs. a stated total),…
ideas.firstMonth: Pull arXiv LaTeX/HTML source for ~20 papers in one subfield, use an LLM to extract (claim, supporting numbers) pairs into a structured table, and write a plain-Python arithmetic checker (percentage/ratio/sum checks) that flags candidate mismatches for manual review.
ideas.experiment: An agent scans a curated set of arXiv physics-ML papers, extracts every pair of numbers that should be arithmetically consistent (a reported percentage improvement vs. the raw before/after numbers, or subgroup counts vs. a stated total), and flags mismatches for human review. The surprising question is what fraction of a 100-paper sample has at least one machine-checkable numeric inconsistency, and whether that rate correlates with venue tier.
ideas.baseline: Each flag is a machine-checkable arithmetic fact (does 23% match (45-37)/37?) independent of any LLM judgment; precision/recall of the auditor is validated against a hand-labeled subsample.
ideas.publicationPath: 6–12 months: scale to 200-500 papers across 3-4 venues/tiers, hand-validate a sample of flagged mismatches to measure the auditor's precision, and publish the mismatch-rate-by-venue findings plus the open-source auditor; target a meta-science/reproducibility workshop.
ideas.risk: LLM extraction of (claim, number) pairs from messy tables/PDFs is itself error-prone; extraction precision must be validated on a hand-labeled subsample before trusting flagged inconsistencies.
ideas.pivot: Use the first month to test whether the proposed comparison is feasible and distinct from earlier work; discuss scope changes with a mentor.
ideas.resources: laptop CPU only; ¥70-150/month cheap LLM API calls for extraction, scaling with corpus size; no GPU
