ideas.title: Calibrated LLM forecasting of a chaotic Lorenz trajectory
ideas.question: How well calibrated are an AI's forecasts of a chaotic Lorenz trajectory?
ideas.hook: A physics student's Lorenz-63 chaotic simulator feeds windowed trajectories to an LLM, which must output a probabilistic forecast for a state variable N steps ahead, scored by CRPS/calibration against the exact deterministic continuation…
ideas.firstMonth: Physics student implements an RK4 Lorenz-63 integrator, verifies the classic butterfly attractor, and numerically estimates the largest Lyapunov exponent; AI student builds the LLM-forecast harness (prompt with a windowed trajectory, parse a predicted distribution) and computes CRPS against ground truth for short horizons.
ideas.experiment: A physics student's Lorenz-63 chaotic simulator feeds windowed trajectories to an LLM, which must output a probabilistic forecast for a state variable N steps ahead, scored by CRPS/calibration against the exact deterministic continuation once revealed. The surprising question is how forecast calibration degrades as the horizon crosses the system's own Lyapunov time, and whether the LLM's stated uncertainty tracks that degradation honestly.
ideas.baseline: The Lorenz-63 system is deterministic given initial conditions and a fixed RNG seed for any noise; the true continuation is always exactly reproducible by re-running the simulator, giving an auto-resolving ground truth for every forecast.
ideas.publicationPath: 6–12 months: sweep forecast horizon relative to Lyapunov time across 2-3 chaotic systems (Lorenz, Rössler, driven pendulum near chaos onset), compare LLM calibration to classical ensemble/particle-filter baselines; target an AI4Science workshop or a nonlinear-dynamics methods paper (Chaos, PRE).
ideas.risk: Chaos means forecast skill decays fast past about one Lyapunov time by construction; the science question must be framed as 'how honest is the reported uncertainty', not 'can the LLM beat chaos', or the result is a foregone conclusion.
ideas.pivot: Center the paper on the single Lyapunov-time-relative calibration-decay curve, not general forecasting accuracy, to separate it from the broader LLM-zero-shot-time-series-forecasting literature that already exists.
ideas.resources: laptop CPU only (Lorenz integration is trivial); ¥70-150/month cheap LLM API calls

originalAssessment.pitch: A physics student's Lorenz-63 chaotic simulator feeds windowed trajectories to an LLM, which must output a probabilistic forecast for a state variable N steps ahead, scored by CRPS/calibration against the exact deterministic continuation once revealed. The surprising question is how forecast calibration degrades as the horizon crosses the system's own Lyapunov time, and whether the LLM's stated uncertainty tracks that degradation honestly.
originalAssessment.groundTruth: The Lorenz-63 system is deterministic given initial conditions and a fixed RNG seed for any noise; the true continuation is always exactly reproducible by re-running the simulator, giving an auto-resolving ground truth for every forecast.

ideas.title: Do LLM novelty scores predict a paper's future citations?
ideas.question: Do AI novelty ratings predict later citation counts?
ideas.hook: An AI student has a cheap LLM rate a large sample of multi-year-old arXiv abstracts on a short novelty/rigor rubric, blind to outcome, then correlates those scores against each paper's actual field-normalized citation impact (OpenAlex's…
ideas.firstMonth: Pull ~200 arXiv abstracts posted 3+ years ago from a fixed subfield via the OpenAlex/arXiv API, write a fixed LLM rubric prompt (novelty, rigor, clarity, 1-5 each), and score all 200 abstracts once, storing raw scores plus metadata with no re-scoring after seeing citations.
ideas.experiment: An AI student has a cheap LLM rate a large sample of multi-year-old arXiv abstracts on a short novelty/rigor rubric, blind to outcome, then correlates those scores against each paper's actual field-normalized citation impact (OpenAlex's Relative Citation Ratio). The surprising question is whether the correlation beats trivial baselines like abstract length or author citation history, or is statistically indistinguishable from them.
ideas.baseline: Citation counts and Relative Citation Ratio are objective, auditable numbers pulled directly from OpenAlex at a fixed snapshot date; LLM scores are logged before the citation pull to prevent leakage/hindsight bias.
ideas.publicationPath: 6–12 months: scale to 1000+ papers across 2-3 subfields, add baselines (abstract length, author citation history, venue) via multiple regression, and test score stability across different cheap LLMs; target a science-of-science workshop or a short note in a quantitative-science-studies journal.
ideas.risk: Any correlation found could be confounded by author fame or venue prestige leaking into the abstract text itself; those must be explicit control variables, not omitted from the regression.
ideas.pivot: Use the first month to test whether the proposed comparison is feasible and distinct from earlier work; discuss scope changes with a mentor.
ideas.resources: laptop CPU only; roughly ¥70-150 total for ~1000 LLM scorings; free OpenAlex API

ideas.title: Agent reconstructs a hidden oscillator network by probing
ideas.question: How efficiently can an agent infer an oscillator network by probing it?
ideas.hook: A physics student's small Kuramoto oscillator network simulator hides a random adjacency matrix, and an agent under a fixed perturb-and-observe query budget must reconstruct that matrix exactly, scored by graph edit distance.
ideas.firstMonth: Physics student implements a Kuramoto network ODE simulator (random sparse adjacency, tunable coupling strength) and a 'perturb node i, return phase trajectories of all nodes' function; AI student wraps this as an agent tool with a hard query-count budget and a naive probe-every-node-once baseline to compare against.
ideas.experiment: A physics student's small Kuramoto oscillator network simulator hides a random adjacency matrix, and an agent under a fixed perturb-and-observe query budget must reconstruct that matrix exactly, scored by graph edit distance. The surprising question is how close an LLM-driven adaptive probing strategy gets to the theoretical minimum-query reconstruction bound from the response-dynamics literature.
ideas.baseline: The true adjacency matrix is known exactly because it was generated by the simulator; graph edit distance to the agent's reconstructed matrix is a fully machine-checkable score, and classical response-dynamics theory gives a provable minimal-query bound to compare against.
ideas.publicationPath: 6–12 months: benchmark agent-designed adaptive probing against the closed-form minimal-query reconstruction bound from response-dynamics theory across network sizes/topologies (random, small-world, scale-free) and test robustness to measurement noise; target a network-science or nonlinear-dynamics venue (Chaos, PRE).
ideas.risk: For very sparse/small networks the reconstruction problem may be too easy to be interesting; the query budget must be pushed toward the information-theoretic minimum (fewer queries than edges) to keep it hard.
ideas.pivot: No paper benchmarks an LLM-driven adaptive prober against the classical minimal-query bound; keep the contribution centered on the query-efficiency gap curve (agent vs. closed-form bound) across topology/noise, since the agent will likely lose and that comparison is the finding.
ideas.resources: laptop CPU only (N≤10 Kuramoto ODEs are trivial); ¥70/month cheap LLM API calls

ideas.question: What misconceptions appear when AI models solve newly written exam questions?
ideas.hook: Compare AI answers to recent exam questions, then organize their mistakes into a misconception taxonomy.
ideas.firstMonth: Collect 30-50 fresh (post-cutoff) Chinese physics-olympiad/gaokao-style problems with answer keys; build a harness that queries the 4 CN LLM APIs and auto-grades numeric/MCQ answers for a first accuracy bar chart by week 2; hand-code wrong answers into a first 5-10-category misconception taxonomy by week 4.
ideas.experiment: Compare several models on recent physics and mathematics exams, then categorize incorrect answers. Recent release dates can reduce some memorization risks, but related training examples and uncertain model training dates prevent a claim that contamination is impossible.
ideas.baseline: Official exam answer keys give exact right/wrong grading for numeric and MCQ items; free-response items get a fixed rubric checked by two independent taggers.
ideas.publicationPath: Grow the benchmark to 300+ items refreshed quarterly, track the accuracy-vs-cutoff-age decay curve across model releases, and publish the benchmark + taxonomy as a dataset/analysis paper; venue: EMNLP/NAACL Findings or an LLM-eval workshop.
ideas.risk: no human subjects (only public exam problems + LLM outputs); main risk is exam copyright/licensing — use only problems the team may legally redistribute or paraphrase Recent exams do not guarantee contamination-free evaluation; source training cutoffs and exposure to related questions may be unknown.
ideas.pivot: Use the first month to test whether the proposed comparison is feasible and distinct from earlier work; discuss scope changes with a mentor.

ideas.title: Socratic vs. direct-answer LLM tutoring: a retention measurement
ideas.question: Does Socratic AI tutoring improve later retention compared with direct answers?
ideas.hook: Build two LLM tutor personas (Socratic question-back vs. direct-answer) and run a within-subject pre/post/delayed-quiz study with consenting volunteer classmates on one physics topic.
ideas.firstMonth: Write the two tutor system prompts, pick one topic (e.g. kinematics) plus a 10-question pre/post quiz bank, get lab-ethics minimal-risk consent signed off, and run a pilot with 6-8 volunteers by week 3; first retention-gap bar chart by week 4.
ideas.experiment: Build two LLM tutor personas (Socratic question-back vs. direct-answer) and run a within-subject pre/post/delayed-quiz study with consenting volunteer classmates on one physics topic. The surprising question: does the recently reported 'metacognitive laziness' effect of GenAI-assisted learning already show up after a single ~20-minute session, and is it fully explained by tutoring style?
ideas.baseline: Quiz items are objectively graded (MCQ/numeric); retention effect size (Cohen's d) is computed from pre/post/delayed scores across randomized tutor-style assignment.
ideas.publicationPath: Scale to ~40-60 consented undergrad volunteers across 2-3 topics over the semester with pre-registered hypotheses and a 1-week delayed post-test; publish a small controlled tutoring-style study; venue: AIED/L@S workshop or a physics-education-research (PERC) proceedings paper.
ideas.risk: human participants — minimal-risk, consent-based (lab-ethics review), voluntary with right to withdraw, anonymized quiz data only, no sensitive personal data collected
ideas.pivot: Use the first month to test whether the proposed comparison is feasible and distinct from earlier work; discuss scope changes with a mentor.
ideas.resources: free-ish: ~¥100 LLM API calls; needs ~2 mentor h/wk to design the consent form and study protocol

ideas.title: Webcam coffee-ring scaling, with a surfactant twist
ideas.question: How does a surfactant change coffee-ring patterns?
ideas.hook: Build a ¥200 webcam+LED time-lapse rig to record evaporating droplets of coffee/ink/salt water on different substrates, measure the ring-deposit radial density profile, and test it against the classic Deegan capillary-flow scaling law,…
ideas.firstMonth: Build the webcam+LED droplet rig, record 10 evaporating coffee/ink droplets at roughly fixed humidity, extract ring-width vs. time via simple image thresholding, and produce a first ring-profile plot by week 3-4.
ideas.experiment: Build a ¥200 webcam+LED time-lapse rig to record evaporating droplets of coffee/ink/salt water on different substrates, measure the ring-deposit radial density profile, and test it against the classic Deegan capillary-flow scaling law, then repeat with a dish-soap surfactant. The surprising question: can a freshman quantify, at home, how much surfactant is needed to measurably suppress or reverse the coffee ring via Marangoni flow, and does the suppression follow a clean scaling law?
ideas.baseline: Deegan capillary-flow theory gives an exact analytic prediction for deposit mass vs. radius/time to compare pixel-intensity-derived profiles against.
ideas.publicationPath: Systematically vary particle concentration, substrate, and surfactant fraction (30+ conditions), fit deposit profiles to the Deegan scaling law and its surfactant-suppressed variant; publish a tabletop soft-matter paper; venue: American Journal of Physics, or Physical Review Fluids / Soft Matter if the surfactant-suppression scaling curve is novel enough.
ideas.risk: no human subjects; minor risk is standard handling of dilute coffee/ink/soap solutions (negligible, no hazardous reagents)
ideas.pivot: Drop the surfactant-suppression scaling claim (established since Still-Yunker-Yodh 2012, restated in the cited 2018 review) and pivot the home-rig twist to something unmeasured at that price point, e.g. substrate-wettability-dependent ring-reversal onset or direct webcam visualization of the Marangoni eddy itself.
ideas.resources: ≤¥300 (webcam, LED ring light, glass slides, coffee/ink/soap), no GPU

ideas.title: Surface-code decoder difficulty map: MWPM vs. union-find
ideas.question: Where do surface-code decoding algorithms differ in accuracy and runtime?
ideas.hook: Use Stim to simulate surface codes across code distance and noise bias (depolarizing vs. biased Pauli noise), decode with PyMatching (MWPM) and a union-find decoder, and build a 2D 'difficulty map' of runtime and logical error rate.
ideas.firstMonth: Install Stim+PyMatching, reproduce a standard surface-code threshold plot (logical vs. physical error rate) by week 2, then add a union-find decoder and a noise-bias sweep by week 4.
ideas.experiment: Use Stim to simulate surface codes across code distance and noise bias (depolarizing vs. biased Pauli noise), decode with PyMatching (MWPM) and a union-find decoder, and build a 2D 'difficulty map' of runtime and logical error rate. The surprising question: exactly where does MWPM's accuracy edge over the much faster union-find decoder become negligible as a function of noise bias, i.e. when is it safe to use the cheap decoder?
ideas.baseline: Stim's noise model and decoder outputs are fully deterministic/simulatable; logical error rate is an exactly computable frequency over many shots — fully machine-checkable.
ideas.publicationPath: Extend the map to circuit-level noise and larger distances (d≤11) with a few GPU/cluster hours, publish a decoder-selection-guide paper with the full difficulty map; venue: Quantum or PRX Quantum, with an APS March Meeting poster as the first rung.
ideas.risk: no human subjects; purely computational, no external risk

originalAssessment.pitch: Run a bit-flip repetition code at several code distances on a free-tier cloud superconducting processor (e.g. IBM Quantum Open Plan), measure the logical error rate vs. distance, and compare against a Stim simulation calibrated from the backend's published qubit error rates. The surprising question: does a small free-tier device already show the qualitative 'break-even' logical-error scaling reported by large in-house surface-code experiments, or does real device crosstalk break the naive scaling before that?
originalAssessment.groundTruth: Repetition-code logical error is measured by exact majority-vote decoding against the known injected bit value — fully machine-checkable; Stim gives an independent theoretical baseline.

ideas.title: How much compute does a neural QEC decoder need to beat MWPM?
ideas.question: How much training compute does a neural quantum-error decoder need to beat a classical one?
ideas.hook: Train a small transformer/GNN decoder for the surface code on Stim-generated circuit-level-noise syndromes using a single GPU, and benchmark its accuracy/speed against MWPM (Sparse Blossom/PyMatching) and union-find in the circuit-noise…
ideas.firstMonth: Generate Stim circuit-level-noise syndrome datasets at small distances (d=3,5), train a small transformer/GNN decoder baseline by week 3, and produce a first accuracy-vs-MWPM comparison plot at d=3 by week 4.
ideas.experiment: Train a small transformer/GNN decoder for the surface code on Stim-generated circuit-level-noise syndromes using a single GPU, and benchmark its accuracy/speed against MWPM (Sparse Blossom/PyMatching) and union-find in the circuit-noise regime where DeepMind's AlphaQubit reported neural decoders beating MWPM. The surprising question: does a compute-budget-constrained (one GPU, no cluster) student decoder ever cross over MWPM's logical error rate, or does the AlphaQubit-style advantage only appear at scales beyond a student budget?
ideas.baseline: Logical error rate under Stim's exactly specified noise model is a fully machine-checkable metric; Sparse Blossom/MWPM gives an exact, well-characterized baseline to beat.
ideas.publicationPath: Scale training to d=7-9 with data augmentation/curriculum learning, map where (if anywhere) the NN decoder crosses over MWPM in the accuracy-speed tradeoff at student-accessible compute, publish a 'minimum compute budget for competitive neural QEC decoding' paper; venue: Quantum, npj Quantum Information, or a NeurIPS ML4PS workshop as the first rung.
ideas.risk: no human subjects; purely computational, no external risk
ideas.pivot: Several 2023-2025 papers already show modest-scale NN decoders approaching MWPM; narrow to an explicit compute-accounting axis nobody has published, e.g. GPU-hours-to-crossover vs code distance at fixed noise, holding architecture fixed.
ideas.resources: 1 GPU (existing lab GPU, ~¥0 marginal), ~¥0-500 if cloud GPU time is rented for the scaling runs
